I wrote the [full Alloy Studio reference research plan](Y:/Rutile3/docs/alloy-studio-reference-research-plan.md) and linked it from the workflow plan.

The recommended first release uses **Codex with your existing sign-in** and a **local Rutile MCP server**. You start from a missing property in the Inspector and copy the task to Codex. Codex searches, downloads sources, runs Python in an isolated research folder, and stages a cited **Phase Data** proposal. Rutile validates it and applies it when you approve. Launching Codex directly from the Inspector comes after that workflow is verified.

The plan defines the four MCP tools, what data leaves the machine, how scripts and evidence are retained, and acceptance tests for each of the five build stages. The first end-to-end test is your Mo–Hf run. It should reproduce the **10.37 g/cm³** computed density estimate, leave elasticity unresolved, and refresh density using the saved equilibrium.

docs/alloy-studio-workflow-plan.md:143:The research plan defines the local MCP tools, the Codex download and extraction workflow, approval in the Inspector, and the Mo–Hf pilot. [Alloy Studio reference research plan](alloy-studio-reference-research-plan.md)
docs/alloy-studio-reference-research-plan.md:3:Add **Find reference** to the Alloy Studio Inspector. Starting from a missing property on a solved phase, Codex searches for sources, downloads the files it needs, and writes and runs Python to extract or calculate a candidate value. Rutile checks the evidence and presents a Phase Data record for review. Applying the record reuses the saved equilibrium and refreshes the affected results.
docs/alloy-studio-reference-research-plan.md:11:**Codex runs the research.** Use the local Codex client and its existing sign-in and permissions. Codex chooses queries, follows papers and supplements, and runs Python in a dedicated research directory. The first release uses **Copy Codex task** from the Inspector. Automatic launch and streamed progress can follow after the manual workflow is verified.
docs/alloy-studio-reference-research-plan.md:13:**Rutile owns the scientific context and the graph.** Add a thin local stdio MCP adapter for the research tools. It calls narrowly scoped endpoints on the existing loopback FastAPI server, which in turn call ordinary Python services. The Inspector calls the same services through the browser API. Keep research state independent of the single active scientific job slot so that searching and downloading can run while a solver job executes. docs/alloy-studio-reference-research-plan.md:15:Rutile needs no OpenAI API key for the Codex path. Both would need their own research execution and retrieval setup. No model provider is required for the scientific application itself. L21: # Prompts
L22: 
L23: Copy page Copy page
L24: 
L25: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardized way for servers to expose prompt templates to clients. Prompts allow servers to provide structured messages and instructions for interacting with language models. Clients can discover available prompts, retrieve their contents, and provide arguments to customize them.
L26: ## User Interaction Model
L27: Prompts are designed to be user-controlled, meaning they are exposed from servers to clients with the intention of the user being able to explicitly select them for use. Typically, prompts would be triggered through user-initiated commands in the user interface, which allows users to naturally discover and invoke available prompts.
L28: For example, as slash commands: 【9†Image: Example of prompt exposed as slash command†mintcdn.com】 However, implementors are free to expose prompts through any interface pattern that suits their needs—the protocol itself does not mandate any specific user interaction model.
L29: ## Capabilities
L30: 
L31: Servers that support prompts MUST declare the `prompts` capability during 【10†initialization】:
L32: 
L33:     `{
L34:       "capabilities": {
L35:         "prompts": {
L36:           "listChanged": true
L37:         }
L38:       }
L39:     }
L40:     `
L41: 
L42: `listChanged` indicates whether the server will emit notifications when the list of available prompts changes.
L43: 
L44: ## Protocol Messages
L45: ### Listing Prompts
L46: 
L47: To retrieve available prompts, clients send a `prompts/list` request. This operation supports 【11†pagination】. Request:
L48: 
L49:     `{
L50:       "jsonrpc": "2.0",
L51:       "id": 1,
L52:       "method": "prompts/list",
L53:       "params": {
L54:         "cursor": "optional-cursor-value"
L55:       }
L56:     }
L57:     `
L58: Response:
L59: 
L60:     `{
L61:       "jsonrpc": "2.0",
L62:       "id": 1,
L63:       "result": {
L64:         "prompts": [
L65:           {
L66:             "name": "code_review",
L67:             "title": "Request Code Review",
L68:             "description": "Asks the LLM to analyze code quality and suggest improvements",
L69:             "arguments": [
L70:               {
L71:                 "name": "code",
L72:                 "description": "The code to review",
L73:                 "required": true
L74:               }
L75:             ],
L76:             "icons": [
L77:               {
L78:                 "src": "https://example.com/review-icon.svg",
L79:                 "mimeType": "image/svg+xml",
L80:                 "sizes": ["any"]
L81:               }
L82:             ]
L83:           }
L84:         ],
L85:         "nextCursor": "next-page-cursor"
L86:       }
L87:     }
L88:     `
L89: ### Getting a Prompt
L90: 
L91: To retrieve a specific prompt, clients send a `prompts/get` request. Arguments may be auto-completed through 【12†the completion API】. Request:
L92: 
L93:     `{
L94:       "jsonrpc": "2.0",
L95:       "id": 2,
L96:       "method": "prompts/get",
L97:       "params": {
L98:         "name": "code_review",
L99:         "arguments": {
L100:           "code": "def hello():\n    print('world')"
L101:         }
L102:       }

L25: Deprecated: The Sampling feature is deprecated as of protocol version `2026-07-28` (【9†SEP-2577†github.com】). Under the 【10†feature lifecycle policy】, it remains in the specification for at least twelve months after this revision’s release before it becomes eligible for removal. New implementations SHOULD NOT adopt it; existing implementations SHOULD migrate to integrating directly with LLM provider APIs. See the 【11†deprecated features registry】.
L26: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardized way for servers to request LLM sampling (“completions” or “generations”) from language models via clients. This flow allows clients to maintain control over model access, selection, and permissions while enabling servers to leverage AI capabilities—with no server API keys necessary. Servers can request text, audio, or image-based interactions and optionally include context from MCP servers in their prompts.
L27: ## User Interaction Model
L28: 
L29: Sampling in MCP allows servers to implement agentic behaviors, by enabling LLM calls to occur nested inside other MCP server features. Implementations are free to expose sampling through any interface pattern that suits their needs—the protocol itself does not mandate any specific user interaction model.
L30: 
L31: For trust & safety and security, there SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny sampling requests.Applications SHOULD:
L32:   * Provide UI that makes it easy and intuitive to review sampling requests
L33:   * Allow users to view and edit prompts before sending
L34:   * Present generated responses for review before delivery
L35: ## Tools in Sampling
L36: Servers can request that the client’s LLM use tools during sampling by providing a `tools` array and optional `toolChoice` configuration in their sampling requests. The tool definitions in the `tools` array are scoped to the sampling request — they don’t need to correspond to registered tools. This enables servers to implement agentic behaviors where the LLM can call specially designated tools, receive results, and continue the conversation - all within a single sampling request flow.
L37: Clients MUST declare support for tool use via the `sampling.tools` capability to receive tool-enabled sampling requests. Servers MUST NOT send tool-enabled sampling requests to Clients that have not declared support for tool use via the `sampling.tools` capability.
L38: ## Capabilities
L39: 
L40: Clients that support sampling MUST declare the `sampling` capability in `_meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities` on each request: Basic sampling:
L41: 
L42:     `{
L43:       "_meta": {
L44:         "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {
L45:           "sampling": {}
L46:         }
L47:       }
L48:     }
L49:     `

L21: # Prompts
L22: 
L23: Copy page Copy page
L24: 
L25: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardized way for servers to expose prompt templates to clients. Prompts allow servers to provide structured messages and instructions for interacting with language models. Clients can discover available prompts, retrieve their contents, and provide arguments to customize them.
L26: ## User Interaction Model
L27: Prompts are designed to be user-controlled, meaning they are exposed from servers to clients with the intention of the user being able to explicitly select them for use. Typically, prompts would be triggered through user-initiated commands in the user interface, which allows users to naturally discover and invoke available prompts.
L28: For example, as slash commands: 【9†Image: Example of prompt exposed as slash command†mintcdn.com】 However, implementors are free to expose prompts through any interface pattern that suits their needs—the protocol itself does not mandate any specific user interaction model.
L29: ## Capabilities
L30: 
L31: Servers that support prompts MUST declare the `prompts` capability during 【10†initialization】:
L32: 
L33:     `{
L34:       "capabilities": {
L35:         "prompts": {
L36:           "listChanged": true
L37:         }
L38:       }
L39:     }
L40:     `
L41: 
L42: `listChanged` indicates whether the server will emit notifications when the list of available prompts changes.
L43: 
L44: ## Protocol Messages
L45: ### Listing Prompts
L46: 
L47: To retrieve available prompts, clients send a `prompts/list` request. This operation supports 【11†pagination】. Request:
L48: 
L49:     `{
L50:       "jsonrpc": "2.0",
L51:       "id": 1,
L52:       "method": "prompts/list",
L53:       "params": {
L54:         "cursor": "optional-cursor-value"
L55:       }
L56:     }
L57:     `
L58: Response:
L59: 
L60:     `{
L61:       "jsonrpc": "2.0",
L62:       "id": 1,
L63:       "result": {
L64:         "prompts": [
L65:           {
L66:             "name": "code_review",
L67:             "title": "Request Code Review",
L68:             "description": "Asks the LLM to analyze code quality and suggest improvements",
L69:             "arguments": [
L70:               {
L71:                 "name": "code",
L72:                 "description": "The code to review",
L73:                 "required": true
L74:               }
L75:             ],
L76:             "icons": [
L77:               {
L78:                 "src": "https://example.com/review-icon.svg",
L79:                 "mimeType": "image/svg+xml",
L80:                 "sizes": ["any"]
L81:               }
L82:             ]
L83:           }
L84:         ],
L85:         "nextCursor": "next-page-cursor"
L86:       }
L87:     }
L88:     `
L89: ### Getting a Prompt
L90: 
L91: To retrieve a specific prompt, clients send a `prompts/get` request. Arguments may be auto-completed through 【12†the completion API】. Request:
L92: 
L93:     `{
L94:       "jsonrpc": "2.0",
L95:       "id": 2,
L96:       "method": "prompts/get",
L97:       "params": {
L98:         "name": "code_review",
L99:         "arguments": {
L100:           "code": "def hello():\n    print('world')"

L21: # Prompts
L22: 
L23: Copy page Copy page
L24: 
L25: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardized way for servers to expose prompt templates to clients. Prompts allow servers to provide structured messages and instructions for interacting with language models. Clients can discover available prompts, retrieve their contents, and provide arguments to customize them.
L26: ## User Interaction Model
L27: Prompts are designed to be user-controlled, meaning they are exposed from servers to clients with the intention of the user being able to explicitly select them for use. Typically, prompts would be triggered through user-initiated commands in the user interface, which allows users to naturally discover and invoke available prompts.
L28: For example, as slash commands: 【9†Image: Example of prompt exposed as slash command†mintcdn.com】 However, implementors are free to expose prompts through any interface pattern that suits their needs—the protocol itself does not mandate any specific user interaction model.
L29: ## Capabilities
L30: 
L31: Servers that support prompts MUST declare the `prompts` capability during 【10†initialization】:
L32: 
L33:     `{
L34:       "capabilities": {
L35:         "prompts": {
L36:           "listChanged": true
L37:         }
L38:       }
L39:     }
L40:     `
L41: 
L42: `listChanged` indicates whether the server will emit notifications when the list of available prompts changes.
L43: 
L44: ## Protocol Messages
L45: ### Listing Prompts
L46: 
L47: To retrieve available prompts, clients send a `prompts/list` request. This operation supports 【11†pagination】. Request:
L48: 
L49:     `{
L50:       "jsonrpc": "2.0",
L51:       "id": 1,
L52:       "method": "prompts/list",
L53:       "params": {
L54:         "cursor": "optional-cursor-value"
L55:       }
L56:     }
L57:     `
L58: Response:
L59: 
L60:     `{
L61:       "jsonrpc": "2.0",
L62:       "id": 1,
L63:       "result": {
L64:         "prompts": [
L65:           {
L66:             "name": "code_review",
L67:             "title": "Request Code Review",
L68:             "description": "Asks the LLM to analyze code quality and suggest improvements",
L69:             "arguments": [
L70:               {
L71:                 "name": "code",
L72:                 "description": "The code to review",
L73:                 "required": true
L74:               }
L75:             ],
L76:             "icons": [
L77:               {
L78:                 "src": "https://example.com/review-icon.svg",
L79:                 "mimeType": "image/svg+xml",
L80:                 "sizes": ["any"]
L81:               }
L82:             ]
L83:           }
L84:         ],
L85:         "nextCursor": "next-page-cursor"
L86:       }
L87:     }
L88:     `
L89: ### Getting a Prompt
L90: 
L91: To retrieve a specific prompt, clients send a `prompts/get` request. Arguments may be auto-completed through 【12†the completion API】. Request:
L92: 
L93:     `{
L94:       "jsonrpc": "2.0",
L95:       "id": 2,
L96:       "method": "prompts/get",
L97:       "params": {
L98:         "name": "code_review",
L99:         "arguments": {
L100:           "code": "def hello():\n    print('world')"
L101:         }
L102:       }

- **`stage_phase_data_proposal` saves a draft for the Inspector.** For Mo–Hf, the agent could submit `10.37 g/cm³`, the source equation and table, the phase conditions, and its Python script. Rutile checks the target and units, copies and hashes the files, and shows what would change. Clicking **Apply** is what updates the graph.
- **MCP can offer a prompt. The host starts the turn.** A compatible host can fetch a Rutile prompt template and let you invoke it. The first version uses **Hand off via MCP → Copy research task**, which works with any connected host that supports the tools. A one-click launch from Rutile would need a host-specific integration, such as Codex App Server’s `turn/start`. [MCP prompts](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/prompts) · [Codex App Server](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app-server)

L170: # pi-mcp-adapter vs Pi's built-in MCP
L171: 
L172: How the adapter differs from the MCP support built into Pi (【58†Pi's MCP docs†pi.dev】), as of Pi 1.3.0. Both read Pi's `mcp.json` files. On Pi 0.99 and later, installing the adapter replaces the built-in in sessions, except when a host supplies its own config through `createMcpAdapter()`; see 【59†Pi's built-in MCP】.
L173: ## In short
L174: 
L175: What you get with the adapter:
L176:   * Idle servers cost nothing. The built-in starts every enabled server in every Pi session and keeps it running until the session ends. By default, the adapter starts a server when the model first calls it and stops it after 10 idle minutes. With 100 servers installed and their tools cached, that's 7.0 GB of server memory against none at session start (【60†measurements】).
L177:   * More servers work fully. Servers can ask you questions through forms, show interactive UIs, offer prompt templates as slash commands, ask the model for a reply, and run long jobs as MCP Tasks (with `"protocolVersion": "auto"`) that keep running in the background while the agent works. The built-in supports none of these.
L178:   * Sign-in tokens go in your OS keychain by default (an encrypted file is opt-in), not in a plain JSON file.
L179:   * Find tools by what you mean. The built-in's `tool_search` only matches words. With a classifier model in Pi, such as Jev or Cloudflare's Clef, the adapter's semantic search ranks tools by meaning: in a test of 12 everyday requests across 95 tools, Jev put the right tool first in 10 of 11, where word search did in 5 (【61†Semantic search】).
L180:   * Adding servers is easier. Give the agent a server's URL and it installs it and checks its tools in the same session, opening sign-in first if the server needs it. Configs from Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, VS Code, and other clients can be imported with `/mcp-adapter setup`, which also adds presets.
L181: What only the built-in has: `codemode` turns on by itself when a server connects. With the adapter, add `"+codemode"` to `defaultTools` in Pi's settings (【62†MCP scripting】). Bulk work across many records also costs less with the built-in: the adapter cost up to 5.5× as much without scripts, where every record passes through the model, and up to 2.9× with `codemode` turned on. Everyday calls cost about the same with both: a single lookup cost 1.8 cents against 2.1 (【63†measurements】).
L182: Pi's `codemode` scripts work with both. Sign-ins made with the built-in can be imported into the adapter; see 【64†Import a sign-in from Pi's built-in MCP】.
L183: ## Running servers
L184:  | Pi's built-in MCP  | pi-mcp-adapter
L185: --- | --- | ---
L186: When servers start and stop  | Pi 1.3.0 connects every enabled server in the background when a session starts and keeps it connected until the session ends; there is no idle stop. The first prompt waits up to 10 seconds only for servers with `direct` tools (【65†Diagnose connection problems†pi.dev】). On Pi 0.99.2, with 100 local test servers, all 100 were still running after 15 minutes (【60†measurements】)  | Started on first use and stopped after 10 idle minutes (the default).
L187: Calls in progress, approvals, and open MCP UI pages keep a server running. When a session starts, servers without cached tools, such as new ones, are started 10 at a time to read their tools, and plain `lazy` servers stop again right after; a server whose discovery failed isn't retried at startup until its command, URL, or another setting that defines it changes. `eager` and `keep-alive` servers start with the session and stay up (【66†How idle shutdown works】, 【67†Lifecycle modes】)
L189:  | Pi's built-in MCP  | pi-mcp-adapter
L190: --- | --- | ---
L191: Add a server  | `pi mcp add` and `pi mcp remove` in a shell, then `/reload` in a running session (【68†Quick setup†pi.dev】)  | In a session: give the agent the URL, and `mcp({ action: "install", url })` connects the server and checks its tools without `/reload`. For an OAuth server it first opens the sign-in page, then checks the tools once you approve. Or use `/mcp-adapter setup`. There's no shell command for adding, but servers added with `pi mcp add` are read (【69†Install from one URL】)
L196: Check servers from a shell  | `pi mcp list`, which exits with status 1 when a server fails (【65†Diagnose connection problems†pi.dev】)  | `pi-mcp-adapter doctor [--json]`, which exits with status 1 when a server fails or needs sign-in, and never starts OAuth (【76†Check servers from a shell】)

L203: Elicitation (a server asks you for input)  | No  | Forms through Pi dialogs, and URL mode in the TUI (【78†MCP elicitation】)
L204: Sampling (a server asks the model for a reply)  | No  | Text only, with a confirmation prompt (【79†Settings】, 【80†Limitations】)

Needs a server that advertises the Tasks extension on an MCP 2026-07-28 connection, so `protocolVersion: "auto"` or `"2026-07-28"` (【81†Task-augmented tool calls】, 【82†Protocol version negotiation】)

L216: On Pi 0.99 and later, scripts call every cached MCP tool by name as `mcp__<server>__<tool>`, direct tools by their own names, and other Pi tools as usual. Pi before 0.99 has no `codemode`, so there are no scripts there (【62†MCP scripting】, 【88†Codemode and tool_search】)

Nothing is added to the model's tool list. Pi 0.99.0 or later (【90†Executor app tools】)

L220:  | Pi's built-in MCP  | pi-mcp-adapter

L53:     `
L54: 
L55: For a remote server:
L56: 
L57:     `pi mcp add docs --url https://example.com/mcp --bearer-token-env-var DOCS_TOKEN
L58:     pi mcp list
L59:     `
L60: These commands add user-level servers by default. Add `--local` or `-l` to write the project configuration instead:
L61: 
L62:     `pi mcp add -l tools --env API_KEY='${TOOLS_KEY}' -- uvx tools-mcp
L63:     `
L64: 
L65: Use `/mcp` inside an interactive session to inspect connections, sign in, reconnect, change exposure, or enable and disable servers. Run `/reload` after adding, removing, or changing a server outside the session.
L66: ## Configure servers
L67: 
L68: Pi reads user-level servers from `~/.pi/agent/mcp.json` and project servers from `.pi/mcp.json`. Project configuration is read only after 【18†project trust】 is granted. A project entry replaces a user-level entry with the same name.
L69: A project entry without `command`, `url`, or `type` overrides only `enabled`, `exposure`, and `toolExposure` of the user-level server with the same name and keeps the rest, including `env`, `headers`, and `auth`. For example, this turns off a user-level server in one project:
L70: 
L71:     `{
L72:       "mcpServers": {
L73:         "internal-tools": { "enabled": false }
L74:       }
L75:     }
L76:     `
L77: The format matches other MCP clients:
L78: 
L79:     `{
L80:       "mcpServers": {
L81:         "filesystem": {
L82:           "command": "npx",
L83:           "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "."]
L84:         },
L85:         "docs": {
L86:           "url": "https://example.com/mcp",
L87:           "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${DOCS_TOKEN}" },
L88:           "description": "Search and read the product documentation"
L89:         }
L90:       }
L91:     }
L92:     `
L108:   * `env` and `headers` values can use environment variables such as `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`. They can also run a command with `!command`, but the command must make up the whole value, for example `"Authorization": "!echo Bearer $(gh auth token)"`.
L109:   * Invalid entries are reported and skipped without preventing other servers from connecting.
L110: `pi mcp add` and `pi mcp remove` cover common changes from a shell. See 【21†MCP commands】 for their options.
L111: ### Inspect or change a server
L112: 
L113: `/mcp` lists configured servers with their state, tool count, exposure, and configuration source. Servers that need attention appear first. Select a server to inspect its tools and connection details, reconnect, sign in or out, change exposure, or enable and disable it.
L114: Exposure and enabled-state changes are saved to the file that defines the server without replacing unrelated content. In a trusted project, "Enable in this project" and "Disable in this project" add a project override for a user-level server; later changes to that server are saved to the override. Disabled servers remain listed. Outside the interactive TUI, `/mcp` prints server status; `/mcp login <server>`, `/mcp logout <server>`, and `/mcp reconnect <server>` perform those actions directly.
L115: Shell commands work without a session: `pi mcp add`, `pi mcp remove`, `pi mcp list`, `pi mcp login`, and `pi mcp logout`. Shell commands do not load extensions.
L116: ### Diagnose connection problems
L117: 
L118: Run `pi mcp list` to connect to every enabled server and print its state, tools, and errors. It exits with status 1 when an entry is invalid or an enabled server is not connected. `/mcp` shows the full connection error and the tail of stderr from a failed stdio server.
L119: Pi reports configuration errors, failed connections, and required sign-ins once after startup. Server logging notifications are appended to `~/.pi/agent/mcp.log` as `<time> [<server>] <level> <logger>: <message>`. The file moves to `mcp.log.1` after it grows past 5 MB.
L120: Pi connects every enabled server in the background when a session starts. A server's tools appear once it connects; the `codemode` description does not list them, so it does not change when servers connect. The first prompt waits up to 10 seconds only for servers with `direct` tools, which must be declared in its request.
L121: Other servers are waited for when they are needed: a codemode script waits for the servers it names (`mcp__<server>`) and, when it calls `searchTools()` or reads `ALL_TOOLS`, for all of them; `tool_search` and the resource tools also wait for all of them. HTTP network errors and transient statuses (408, 429, and 5xx) are retried twice. A dropped connection is shown as disconnected and reconnects on the next call.
L124: ## Migrate configuration from another client
L125: 
L126: Move the converted entry under `mcpServers` in `mcp.json`, then run `pi mcp list` to validate it.
L143: When the server rejects an unauthenticated connection, `/mcp` shows that it needs sign-in. Select "Sign in", run `/mcp login sentry`, or run `pi mcp login sentry`. Pi opens the authorization page and waits for approval. If the browser runs on another machine, such as over SSH, paste its redirected URL into the sign-in screen. A running session uses the new credentials on its next turn.
L179: `pi mcp add --oauth-client-registration <mode>` sets it when adding a server. `cimd` cannot be combined with `clientId` or `clientName`, and a `callbackUrl` must use `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` with the path `/callback`.

L170: # pi-mcp-adapter vs Pi's built-in MCP
L171: 
L172: How the adapter differs from the MCP support built into Pi (【58†Pi's MCP docs†pi.dev】), as of Pi 1.3.0. Both read Pi's `mcp.json` files. On Pi 0.99 and later, installing the adapter replaces the built-in in sessions, except when a host supplies its own config through `createMcpAdapter()`; see 【59†Pi's built-in MCP】.
L173: ## In short
L174: 
L175: What you get with the adapter:
L176:   * Idle servers cost nothing. The built-in starts every enabled server in every Pi session and keeps it running until the session ends. By default, the adapter starts a server when the model first calls it and stops it after 10 idle minutes. With 100 servers installed and their tools cached, that's 7.0 GB of server memory against none at session start (【60†measurements】).
L177:   * More servers work fully. Servers can ask you questions through forms, show interactive UIs, offer prompt templates as slash commands, ask the model for a reply, and run long jobs as MCP Tasks (with `"protocolVersion": "auto"`) that keep running in the background while the agent works. The built-in supports none of these.
L178:   * Sign-in tokens go in your OS keychain by default (an encrypted file is opt-in), not in a plain JSON file.
L179:   * Find tools by what you mean. The built-in's `tool_search` only matches words. With a classifier model in Pi, such as Jev or Cloudflare's Clef, the adapter's semantic search ranks tools by meaning: in a test of 12 everyday requests across 95 tools, Jev put the right tool first in 10 of 11, where word search did in 5 (【61†Semantic search】).
L180:   * Adding servers is easier. Give the agent a server's URL and it installs it and checks its tools in the same session, opening sign-in first if the server needs it. Configs from Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, VS Code, and other clients can be imported with `/mcp-adapter setup`, which also adds presets.
L181: What only the built-in has: `codemode` turns on by itself when a server connects. With the adapter, add `"+codemode"` to `defaultTools` in Pi's settings (【62†MCP scripting】). Bulk work across many records also costs less with the built-in: the adapter cost up to 5.5× as much without scripts, where every record passes through the model, and up to 2.9× with `codemode` turned on. Everyday calls cost about the same with both: a single lookup cost 1.8 cents against 2.1 (【63†measurements】).
L182: Pi's `codemode` scripts work with both. Sign-ins made with the built-in can be imported into the adapter; see 【64†Import a sign-in from Pi's built-in MCP】.
L183: ## Running servers
L184:  | Pi's built-in MCP  | pi-mcp-adapter
L185: --- | --- | ---
L186: When servers start and stop  | Pi 1.3.0 connects every enabled server in the background when a session starts and keeps it connected until the session ends; there is no idle stop. The first prompt waits up to 10 seconds only for servers with `direct` tools (【65†Diagnose connection problems†pi.dev】). On Pi 0.99.2, with 100 local test servers, all 100 were still running after 15 minutes (【60†measurements】)  | Started on first use and stopped after 10 idle minutes (the default).
L187: Calls in progress, approvals, and open MCP UI pages keep a server running. When a session starts, servers without cached tools, such as new ones, are started 10 at a time to read their tools, and plain `lazy` servers stop again right after; a server whose discovery failed isn't retried at startup until its command, URL, or another setting that defines it changes. `eager` and `keep-alive` servers start with the session and stay up (【66†How idle shutdown works】, 【67†Lifecycle modes】)
L189:  | Pi's built-in MCP  | pi-mcp-adapter
L190: --- | --- | ---
L191: Add a server  | `pi mcp add` and `pi mcp remove` in a shell, then `/reload` in a running session (【68†Quick setup†pi.dev】)  | In a session: give the agent the URL, and `mcp({ action: "install", url })` connects the server and checks its tools without `/reload`. For an OAuth server it first opens the sign-in page, then checks the tools once you approve. Or use `/mcp-adapter setup`. There's no shell command for adding, but servers added with `pi mcp add` are read (【69†Install from one URL】)
L196: Check servers from a shell  | `pi mcp list`, which exits with status 1 when a server fails (【65†Diagnose connection problems†pi.dev】)  | `pi-mcp-adapter doctor [--json]`, which exits with status 1 when a server fails or needs sign-in, and never starts OAuth (【76†Check servers from a shell】)
L200:  | Pi's built-in MCP  | pi-mcp-adapter
L201: --- | --- | ---
L202: Prompts (templates a server offers)  | No  | Slash commands `/mcp__<server>__<prompt>` (【77†MCP prompts】)
L203: Elicitation (a server asks you for input)  | No  | Forms through Pi dialogs, and URL mode in the TUI (【78†MCP elicitation】)
L204: Sampling (a server asks the model for a reply)  | No  | Text only, with a confirmation prompt (【79†Settings】, 【80†Limitations】)
L205: Tasks (long-running tool calls)  | No  | The job runs in the background while the agent keeps working, and the result comes back on its own. Needs a server that advertises the Tasks extension on an MCP 2026-07-28 connection, so `protocolVersion: "auto"` or `"2026-07-28"` (【81†Task-augmented tool calls】, 【82†Protocol version negotiation】)
L206: MCP UI (interactive tool pages)  | UI resources are left out (【83†Use resources†pi.dev】)  | Tool UIs open in a native macOS window or the browser and can call tools (【84†MCP UI integration】)
L207: Resources (data a server exposes)  | `list_mcp_resources`, `list_mcp_resource_templates`, and `read_mcp_resource` tools (【83†Use resources†pi.dev】)  | Resources exposed as tools, on by default (`exposeResources`) (【79†Settings】)

L209: Server log messages  | Appended to `~/.pi/agent/mcp.log`  | Appended to the same file, in the same format
L211:  | Pi's built-in MCP  | pi-mcp-adapter
L212: --- | --- | ---
L213: Tool search  | `tool_search` finds and loads tools with `deferred` exposure, ranked by words (BM25). A server's `exposure` and per-tool `toolExposure` decide which tools it covers, and a server's `description` helps rank its tools (【86†Control tool exposure†pi.dev】, 【87†Tool search†pi.dev】)  | On Pi 0.99 and later, every cached MCP tool is a Pi deferred tool, so `tool_search` finds them all; tools of servers set to `directTools: "search"` keep their own names.
L214: `mcp({ search })` also ranks tools by words or matches them by regex. `searchMode: "semantic"` has a Pi classifier model, such as Jev, rank tools by meaning, using Pi's own logins; it's used only when a search asks for it (【88†Codemode and tool_search】, 【61†Semantic search】)

Scripts call MCP tools by name, and any other Pi tool such as `bash` or `read` (【86†Control tool exposure†pi.dev】)  | Pi's `codemode` is the only way to script MCP calls, and it isn't turned on automatically: add `"+codemode"` to `defaultTools` in Pi's settings.
L216: On Pi 0.99 and later, scripts call every cached MCP tool by name as `mcp__<server>__<tool>`, direct tools by their own names, and other Pi tools as usual. Pi before 0.99 has no `codemode`, so there are no scripts there (【62†MCP scripting】, 【88†Codemode and tool_search】)

L43: # MCP Servers
L44: 
L45: Pi connects to 【17†Model Context Protocol†modelcontextprotocol.io】 servers over stdio or streamable HTTP and makes their tools and resources available to the model.
L46: ## Quick setup
L47: 
L48: Add a local stdio server, check the connection, then start Pi:
L49: 
L50:     `pi mcp add filesystem -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem .
L51:     pi mcp list
L52:     pi
L53:     `
L54: 
L55: For a remote server:
L56: 
L57:     `pi mcp add docs --url https://example.com/mcp --bearer-token-env-var DOCS_TOKEN
L58:     pi mcp list
L59:     `
L60: These commands add user-level servers by default. Add `--local` or `-l` to write the project configuration instead:
L61: 
L62:     `pi mcp add -l tools --env API_KEY='${TOOLS_KEY}' -- uvx tools-mcp
L63:     `
L64: 
L65: Use `/mcp` inside an interactive session to inspect connections, sign in, reconnect, change exposure, or enable and disable servers. Run `/reload` after adding, removing, or changing a server outside the session.
L66: ## Configure servers
L67: 
L68: Pi reads user-level servers from `~/.pi/agent/mcp.json` and project servers from `.pi/mcp.json`. Project configuration is read only after 【18†project trust】 is granted. A project entry replaces a user-level entry with the same name.
L69: A project entry without `command`, `url`, or `type` overrides only `enabled`, `exposure`, and `toolExposure` of the user-level server with the same name and keeps the rest, including `env`, `headers`, and `auth`. For example, this turns off a user-level server in one project:
L70: 
L71:     `{
L72:       "mcpServers": {
L73:         "internal-tools": { "enabled": false }
L74:       }
L75:     }
L76:     `
L77: The format matches other MCP clients:
L78: 
L79:     `{
L80:       "mcpServers": {
L81:         "filesystem": {
L82:           "command": "npx",
L83:           "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "."]
L84:         },
L85:         "docs": {
L86:           "url": "https://example.com/mcp",
L87:           "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${DOCS_TOKEN}" },
L88:           "description": "Search and read the product documentation"
L89:         }
L90:       }
L91:     }
L92:     `
L108:   * `env` and `headers` values can use environment variables such as `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`. They can also run a command with `!command`, but the command must make up the whole value, for example `"Authorization": "!echo Bearer $(gh auth token)"`.
L109:   * Invalid entries are reported and skipped without preventing other servers from connecting.
L110: `pi mcp add` and `pi mcp remove` cover common changes from a shell. See 【21†MCP commands】 for their options.
L111: ### Inspect or change a server
L112: 
L113: `/mcp` lists configured servers with their state, tool count, exposure, and configuration source. Servers that need attention appear first. Select a server to inspect its tools and connection details, reconnect, sign in or out, change exposure, or enable and disable it.
L114: Exposure and enabled-state changes are saved to the file that defines the server without replacing unrelated content. In a trusted project, "Enable in this project" and "Disable in this project" add a project override for a user-level server; later changes to that server are saved to the override. Disabled servers remain listed. Outside the interactive TUI, `/mcp` prints server status; `/mcp login <server>`, `/mcp logout <server>`, and `/mcp reconnect <server>` perform those actions directly.
L115: Shell commands work without a session: `pi mcp add`, `pi mcp remove`, `pi mcp list`, `pi mcp login`, and `pi mcp logout`. Shell commands do not load extensions.
L116: ### Diagnose connection problems
L117: 
L118: Run `pi mcp list` to connect to every enabled server and print its state, tools, and errors. It exits with status 1 when an entry is invalid or an enabled server is not connected. `/mcp` shows the full connection error and the tail of stderr from a failed stdio server.
L119: Pi reports configuration errors, failed connections, and required sign-ins once after startup. Server logging notifications are appended to `~/.pi/agent/mcp.log` as `<time> [<server>] <level> <logger>: <message>`. The file moves to `mcp.log.1` after it grows past 5 MB.
L120: Pi connects every enabled server in the background when a session starts. A server's tools appear once it connects; the `codemode` description does not list them, so it does not change when servers connect. The first prompt waits up to 10 seconds only for servers with `direct` tools, which must be declared in its request.
L121: Other servers are waited for when they are needed: a codemode script waits for the servers it names (`mcp__<server>`) and, when it calls `searchTools()` or reads `ALL_TOOLS`, for all of them; `tool_search` and the resource tools also wait for all of them. HTTP network errors and transient statuses (408, 429, and 5xx) are retried twice. A dropped connection is shown as disconnected and reconnects on the next call.
L124: ## Migrate configuration from another client
L125: 
L126: Move the converted entry under `mcpServers` in `mcp.json`, then run `pi mcp list` to validate it.
L143: When the server rejects an unauthenticated connection, `/mcp` shows that it needs sign-in. Select "Sign in", run `/mcp login sentry`, or run `pi mcp login sentry`. Pi opens the authorization page and waits for approval. If the browser runs on another machine, such as over SSH, paste its redirected URL into the sign-in screen. A running session uses the new credentials on its next turn.
L179: `pi mcp add --oauth-client-registration <mode>` sets it when adding a server. `cimd` cannot be combined with `clientId` or `clientName`, and a `callbackUrl` must use `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` with the path `/callback`.

L170: # pi-mcp-adapter vs Pi's built-in MCP
L171: 
L172: How the adapter differs from the MCP support built into Pi (【58†Pi's MCP docs†pi.dev】), as of Pi 1.3.0. Both read Pi's `mcp.json` files. On Pi 0.99 and later, installing the adapter replaces the built-in in sessions, except when a host supplies its own config through `createMcpAdapter()`; see 【59†Pi's built-in MCP】.
L173: ## In short
L174: 
L175: What you get with the adapter:
L176:   * Idle servers cost nothing. The built-in starts every enabled server in every Pi session and keeps it running until the session ends. By default, the adapter starts a server when the model first calls it and stops it after 10 idle minutes. With 100 servers installed and their tools cached, that's 7.0 GB of server memory against none at session start (【60†measurements】).
L177:   * More servers work fully. Servers can ask you questions through forms, show interactive UIs, offer prompt templates as slash commands, ask the model for a reply, and run long jobs as MCP Tasks (with `"protocolVersion": "auto"`) that keep running in the background while the agent works. The built-in supports none of these.
L178:   * Sign-in tokens go in your OS keychain by default (an encrypted file is opt-in), not in a plain JSON file.
L179:   * Find tools by what you mean. The built-in's `tool_search` only matches words. With a classifier model in Pi, such as Jev or Cloudflare's Clef, the adapter's semantic search ranks tools by meaning: in a test of 12 everyday requests across 95 tools, Jev put the right tool first in 10 of 11, where word search did in 5 (【61†Semantic search】).
L180:   * Adding servers is easier. Give the agent a server's URL and it installs it and checks its tools in the same session, opening sign-in first if the server needs it. Configs from Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, VS Code, and other clients can be imported with `/mcp-adapter setup`, which also adds presets.
L181: What only the built-in has: `codemode` turns on by itself when a server connects. With the adapter, add `"+codemode"` to `defaultTools` in Pi's settings (【62†MCP scripting】). Bulk work across many records also costs less with the built-in: the adapter cost up to 5.5× as much without scripts, where every record passes through the model, and up to 2.9× with `codemode` turned on. Everyday calls cost about the same with both: a single lookup cost 1.8 cents against 2.1 (【63†measurements】).
L182: Pi's `codemode` scripts work with both. Sign-ins made with the built-in can be imported into the adapter; see 【64†Import a sign-in from Pi's built-in MCP】.
L183: ## Running servers
L184:  | Pi's built-in MCP  | pi-mcp-adapter
L185: --- | --- | ---
L186: When servers start and stop  | Pi 1.3.0 connects every enabled server in the background when a session starts and keeps it connected until the session ends; there is no idle stop. The first prompt waits up to 10 seconds only for servers with `direct` tools (【65†Diagnose connection problems†pi.dev】). On Pi 0.99.2, with 100 local test servers, all 100 were still running after 15 minutes (【60†measurements】)  | Started on first use and stopped after 10 idle minutes (the default).
L187: Calls in progress, approvals, and open MCP UI pages keep a server running. When a session starts, servers without cached tools, such as new ones, are started 10 at a time to read their tools, and plain `lazy` servers stop again right after; a server whose discovery failed isn't retried at startup until its command, URL, or another setting that defines it changes. `eager` and `keep-alive` servers start with the session and stay up (【66†How idle shutdown works】, 【67†Lifecycle modes】)
L189:  | Pi's built-in MCP  | pi-mcp-adapter
L190: --- | --- | ---
L191: Add a server  | `pi mcp add` and `pi mcp remove` in a shell, then `/reload` in a running session (【68†Quick setup†pi.dev】)  | In a session: give the agent the URL, and `mcp({ action: "install", url })` connects the server and checks its tools without `/reload`. For an OAuth server it first opens the sign-in page, then checks the tools once you approve. Or use `/mcp-adapter setup`. There's no shell command for adding, but servers added with `pi mcp add` are read (【69†Install from one URL】)
L196: Check servers from a shell  | `pi mcp list`, which exits with status 1 when a server fails (【65†Diagnose connection problems†pi.dev】)  | `pi-mcp-adapter doctor [--json]`, which exits with status 1 when a server fails or needs sign-in, and never starts OAuth (【76†Check servers from a shell】)
L200:  | Pi's built-in MCP  | pi-mcp-adapter
L201: --- | --- | ---
L202: Prompts (templates a server offers)  | No  | Slash commands `/mcp__<server>__<prompt>` (【77†MCP prompts】)
L203: Elicitation (a server asks you for input)  | No  | Forms through Pi dialogs, and URL mode in the TUI (【78†MCP elicitation】)
L204: Sampling (a server asks the model for a reply)  | No  | Text only, with a confirmation prompt (【79†Settings】, 【80†Limitations】)
L205: Tasks (long-running tool calls)  | No  | The job runs in the background while the agent keeps working, and the result comes back on its own. Needs a server that advertises the Tasks extension on an MCP 2026-07-28 connection, so `protocolVersion: "auto"` or `"2026-07-28"` (【81†Task-augmented tool calls】, 【82†Protocol version negotiation】)
L206: MCP UI (interactive tool pages)  | UI resources are left out (【83†Use resources†pi.dev】)  | Tool UIs open in a native macOS window or the browser and can call tools (【84†MCP UI integration】)
L207: Resources (data a server exposes)  | `list_mcp_resources`, `list_mcp_resource_templates`, and `read_mcp_resource` tools (【83†Use resources†pi.dev】)  | Resources exposed as tools, on by default (`exposeResources`) (【79†Settings】)
L208: Roots (the session directory, sent to servers)  | Sent  | Sent; `"roots": false` turns it off for one server (【85†Fields】)
L209: Server log messages  | Appended to `~/.pi/agent/mcp.log`  | Appended to the same file, in the same format
L211:  | Pi's built-in MCP  | pi-mcp-adapter
L212: --- | --- | ---
L213: Tool search  | `tool_search` finds and loads tools with `deferred` exposure, ranked by words (BM25). A server's `exposure` and per-tool `toolExposure` decide which tools it covers, and a server's `description` helps rank its tools (【86†Control tool exposure†pi.dev】, 【87†Tool search†pi.dev】)  | On Pi 0.99 and later, every cached MCP tool is a Pi deferred tool, so `tool_search` finds them all; tools of servers set to `directTools: "search"` keep their own names.
L214: `mcp({ search })` also ranks tools by words or matches them by regex. `searchMode: "semantic"` has a Pi classifier model, such as Jev, rank tools by meaning, using Pi's own logins; it's used only when a search asks for it (【88†Codemode and tool_search】, 【61†Semantic search】)
L215: Scripts that call many tools  | Pi's `codemode` tool, turned on when a server with the default `codemode` exposure connects; `autoEnableCodemode: false` stops that, and `codemode.mode` decides how other tools are presented. Scripts call MCP tools by name, and any other Pi tool such as `bash` or `read` (【86†Control tool exposure†pi.dev】)  | Pi's `codemode` is the only way to script MCP calls, and it isn't turned on automatically: add `"+codemode"` to `defaultTools` in Pi's settings.
L216: On Pi 0.99 and later, scripts call every cached MCP tool by name as `mcp__<server>__<tool>`, direct tools by their own names, and other Pi tools as usual. Pi before 0.99 has no `codemode`, so there are no scripts there (【62†MCP scripting】, 【88†Codemode and tool_search】)
L217: Saved workflows as tools  | No. A `codemode` script runs once, and the model writes it again each time  | `scriptTools` saves a script as a tool with its own name, description and input schema. It runs in Pi's `codemode`, calls MCP and Pi tools, and is found by search and called like any other tool. Pi 0.99.0 or later (【89†Script tools】)
L218: Executor app tools  | Only the six tools Executor itself lists; the model reaches app tools through Executor's `search` and `call`  | On Executor's default URL, each app tool is a Pi deferred tool named `mcp__<server>__<app>_<tool>`, up to 1,000 per Executor server, found by `tool_search` and `mcp({ search })` and called by name with `approveTools` matching its path. Nothing is added to the model's tool list. Pi 0.99.0 or later (【90†Executor app tools】)
L219: ## Security
L220:  | Pi's built-in MCP  | pi-mcp-adapter
L221: --- | --- | ---
L222: OAuth token storage  | A JSON file, `~/.pi/agent/mcp-auth.json`, created with mode 0600 (【91†OAuth†pi.dev】)  | The OS credential store: macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or Linux Secret Service. No plaintext fallback; an encrypted file store is opt-in (【92†Token storage】)
L223: Asking before risky tools  | Every MCP call goes through Pi's tool pipeline, so permission extensions see each tool and its annotations (【93†Permissions†pi.dev】)  | `approveTools` asks before matching tools run. On Pi 0.99 and later, calls through `mcp` and `mcp__<server>` and from `codemode` scripts also run as Pi tool calls under the tool's own name, so permission extensions see each tool and its annotations; direct tools are seen under their own names.
L224: A call that stays inside the proxy, such as under `MCP_DIRECT_TOOLS=__none__`, is one call to `mcp`, and a call from another extension through the runtime tool-call event reaches no Pi hook; an extension that wants those MCP calls uses the adapter's approval broker event (【94†Tool approval】, 【88†Codemode and tool_search】)
L225: ## Connections
L226: 
L227:  | Pi's built-in MCP  | pi-mcp-adapter
L228: --- | --- | ---
L229: Transports  | stdio and streamable HTTP; SSE is rejected (【95†Configuration rules†pi.dev】)  | stdio and streamable HTTP, with fallback to legacy SSE, plus an `rmcp-mux` Unix-domain socket (【85†Fields】, 【96†rmcp-mux】)
L230: Servers from other extensions  | `pi.registerMcpServer()` (【97†Add servers from extensions†pi.dev】)  | Connects those servers on Pi 0.99 and later, through the proxy only (【98†Runtime registration】)
L231: ## Measured with 100 servers
L232: 
L233: Measured on Pi 0.99.2. 100 local test servers with 50 tools each, Node 25.2.1, Apple M4 Pro, macOS 15.6. The adapter had cached tools from an earlier session, and 3 servers were used.
L234:  | Pi 0.99.2 built-in  | pi-mcp-adapter
L235: --- | --- | ---
L236: Servers running at session start  | 100  | 0
L237: Servers running while 3 are used  | 100  | 3
L238: Servers running after the idle timeout  | 100 (checked after 15 minutes)  | 0
L239: Server memory at session start  | 7.0 GB  | 0
L240: Server memory after 15 minutes  | 5.9 GB  | 0 once idle servers stop
L241:   * First session, no cached tools: the adapter starts servers 10 at a time to read their tools and stops each one right after. The session was ready in about 2 s with 0 servers running.

L43: # MCP Servers
L44: 
L45: Pi connects to 【17†Model Context Protocol†modelcontextprotocol.io】 servers over stdio or streamable HTTP and makes their tools and resources available to the model.
L46: ## Quick setup
L47: 
L48: Add a local stdio server, check the connection, then start Pi:
L49: 
L50:     `pi mcp add filesystem -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem .
L51:     pi mcp list
L52:     pi
L53:     `
L54: 
L55: For a remote server:
L56: 
L57:     `pi mcp add docs --url https://example.com/mcp --bearer-token-env-var DOCS_TOKEN
L58:     pi mcp list
L59:     `
L60: These commands add user-level servers by default. Add `--local` or `-l` to write the project configuration instead:
L61: 
L62:     `pi mcp add -l tools --env API_KEY='${TOOLS_KEY}' -- uvx tools-mcp
L63:     `
L64: 
L65: Use `/mcp` inside an interactive session to inspect connections, sign in, reconnect, change exposure, or enable and disable servers. Run `/reload` after adding, removing, or changing a server outside the session.
L66: ## Configure servers
L67: 
L68: Pi reads user-level servers from `~/.pi/agent/mcp.json` and project servers from `.pi/mcp.json`. Project configuration is read only after 【18†project trust】 is granted. A project entry replaces a user-level entry with the same name.
L69: A project entry without `command`, `url`, or `type` overrides only `enabled`, `exposure`, and `toolExposure` of the user-level server with the same name and keeps the rest, including `env`, `headers`, and `auth`. For example, this turns off a user-level server in one project:
L70: 
L71:     `{
L72:       "mcpServers": {
L73:         "internal-tools": { "enabled": false }
L74:       }
L75:     }
L76:     `
L77: The format matches other MCP clients:
L78: 
L79:     `{
L80:       "mcpServers": {
L81:         "filesystem": {
L82:           "command": "npx",
L83:           "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "."]
L84:         },
L85:         "docs": {
L86:           "url": "https://example.com/mcp",
L87:           "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${DOCS_TOKEN}" },
L88:           "description": "Search and read the product documentation"
L89:         }
L90:       }
L91:     }
L92:     `
L108:   * `env` and `headers` values can use environment variables such as `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`. They can also run a command with `!command`, but the command must make up the whole value, for example `"Authorization": "!echo Bearer $(gh auth token)"`.
L109:   * Invalid entries are reported and skipped without preventing other servers from connecting.
L110: `pi mcp add` and `pi mcp remove` cover common changes from a shell. See 【21†MCP commands】 for their options.
L111: ### Inspect or change a server
L112: 
L113: `/mcp` lists configured servers with their state, tool count, exposure, and configuration source. Servers that need attention appear first. Select a server to inspect its tools and connection details, reconnect, sign in or out, change exposure, or enable and disable it.
L114: Exposure and enabled-state changes are saved to the file that defines the server without replacing unrelated content. In a trusted project, "Enable in this project" and "Disable in this project" add a project override for a user-level server; later changes to that server are saved to the override. Disabled servers remain listed. Outside the interactive TUI, `/mcp` prints server status; `/mcp login <server>`, `/mcp logout <server>`, and `/mcp reconnect <server>` perform those actions directly.
L115: Shell commands work without a session: `pi mcp add`, `pi mcp remove`, `pi mcp list`, `pi mcp login`, and `pi mcp logout`. Shell commands do not load extensions.
L116: ### Diagnose connection problems
L117: 
L118: Run `pi mcp list` to connect to every enabled server and print its state, tools, and errors. It exits with status 1 when an entry is invalid or an enabled server is not connected. `/mcp` shows the full connection error and the tail of stderr from a failed stdio server.
L119: Pi reports configuration errors, failed connections, and required sign-ins once after startup. Server logging notifications are appended to `~/.pi/agent/mcp.log` as `<time> [<server>] <level> <logger>: <message>`. The file moves to `mcp.log.1` after it grows past 5 MB.
L120: Pi connects every enabled server in the background when a session starts. A server's tools appear once it connects; the `codemode` description does not list them, so it does not change when servers connect. The first prompt waits up to 10 seconds only for servers with `direct` tools, which must be declared in its request.
L121: Other servers are waited for when they are needed: a codemode script waits for the servers it names (`mcp__<server>`) and, when it calls `searchTools()` or reads `ALL_TOOLS`, for all of them; `tool_search` and the resource tools also wait for all of them. HTTP network errors and transient statuses (408, 429, and 5xx) are retried twice. A dropped connection is shown as disconnected and reconnects on the next call.
L124: ## Migrate configuration from another client
L125: 
L126: Move the converted entry under `mcpServers` in `mcp.json`, then run `pi mcp list` to validate it.
L143: When the server rejects an unauthenticated connection, `/mcp` shows that it needs sign-in. Select "Sign in", run `/mcp login sentry`, or run `pi mcp login sentry`. Pi opens the authorization page and waits for approval. If the browser runs on another machine, such as over SSH, paste its redirected URL into the sign-in screen. A running session uses the new credentials on its next turn.
L179: `pi mcp add --oauth-client-registration <mode>` sets it when adding a server. `cimd` cannot be combined with `clientId` or `clientName`, and a `callbackUrl` must use `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` with the path `/callback`.

L165: The format matches other MCP clients:
L166: 
L167:     `{
L168:       "mcpServers": {
L169:         "filesystem": {
L170:           "command": "npx",
L171:           "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "."]
L172:         },
L173:         "docs": {
L174:           "url": "https://example.com/mcp",
L175:           "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${DOCS_TOKEN}" },
L176:           "description": "Search and read the product documentation"
L177:         }
L178:       }
L179:     }`
L180: Stdio servers use `command`, `args`, `env`, and `cwd`. Relative `cwd` values resolve against the session directory. A leading `~/` in `command`, an argument, or `cwd` names the home directory.
L181: 
L182: HTTP servers use `url`, `headers`, and `oauth` (see 【49†Authenticate with OAuth】). The legacy SSE transport is not supported.
L183: 
L184: Both server types support:
L185:   * `timeout`: per-request timeout in seconds (default 60). Progress notifications reset it.
L186:   * `enabled: false`: keep the entry without connecting to it.
L187:   * `exposure` and `toolExposure`: control how tools reach the model (see 【50†Control tool exposure】).
L188:   * `description`: what the server offers, in a sentence. Without it, the first line of the server instructions is used once the server connects.
L189: Keep personal servers and servers with credentials in the user-level file. Use the project file only for servers the project requires, and only in trusted projects.
L190: ### Configuration rules
L191:   * Server names may contain only letters, digits, `_`, and `-`. Tools are named `mcp__<server>__<tool>`, with every character other than letters, digits, and `_` replaced by `_`; tools of a server whose names then collide all get a hash suffix. L195:   * `env` and `headers` values can use environment variables such as `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`. They can also run a command with `!command`, but the command must make up the whole value, for example `"Authorization": "!echo Bearer $(gh auth token)"`.

L203: ### Diagnose connection problems
L204: 
L205: Run `pi mcp list` to connect to every enabled server and print its state, tools, and errors. It exits with status 1 when an entry is invalid or an enabled server is not connected. `/mcp` shows the full connection error and the tail of stderr from a failed stdio server.

L207: Pi connects every enabled server in the background when a session starts. L212: 
L213: Move the converted entry under `mcpServers` in `mcp.json`, then run `pi mcp list` to validate it.

L215: --- | ---
L216: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or Cursor  | Copy the existing `mcpServers` entry.
L217: VS Code  | Move an entry from the top-level `servers` object and replace `${input:...}` prompts with `${NAME}` environment variables.

L221: 
L222: Remote servers that use OAuth, such as Sentry, need no credentials in `mcp.json`:
L223: 
L224:     `{
L225:       "mcpServers": {
L226:         "sentry": { "url": "https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp" }
L227:       }
L228:     }`

L180: Stdio servers use `command`, `args`, `env`, and `cwd`. Relative `cwd` values resolve against the session directory. A leading `~/` in `command`, an argument, or `cwd` names the home directory.
L181: 
L182: HTTP servers use `url`, `headers`, and `oauth` (see 【49†Authenticate with OAuth】). The legacy SSE transport is not supported.
L183: 
L184: Both server types support:
L185:   * `timeout`: per-request timeout in seconds (default 60). Progress notifications reset it.
L186:   * `enabled: false`: keep the entry without connecting to it.
L187:   * `exposure` and `toolExposure`: control how tools reach the model (see 【50†Control tool exposure】).
L188:   * `description`: what the server offers, in a sentence. It lists the server in the system prompt (see 【50†Control tool exposure】), tool search ranks the server's tools by it, and codemode's `describeNamespace()` returns it. Without it, the first line of the server instructions is used once the server connects.
L189: Keep personal servers and servers with credentials in the user-level file. Use the project file only for servers the project requires, and only in trusted projects.
L190: ### Configuration rules
L191:   * Server names may contain only letters, digits, `_`, and `-`. Tools are named `mcp__<server>__<tool>`, with every character other than letters, digits, and `_` replaced by `_`; tools of a server whose names then collide all get a hash suffix. Server names that differ only in `-` and `_` count as the same server: a second one is rejected, and a `mcp.json` server overrides a registered one.
L192:   * `type` is optional. A `command` selects stdio and a `url` selects streamable HTTP. When present, `type` must be `stdio`, `http`, or `streamable-http`.
L193:   * `sse` is rejected. Servers that document an SSE endpoint often also provide streamable HTTP, commonly at `/mcp` instead of `/sse`.
L194:   * `command` is one executable and `args` contains its arguments. It is not a shell command string.
L195:   * `env` and `headers` values can use environment variables such as `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`. They can also run a command with `!command`, but the command must make up the whole value, for example `"Authorization": "!echo Bearer $(gh auth token)"`.
L196:   * Invalid entries are reported and skipped without preventing other servers from connecting.
L197: `pi mcp add` and `pi mcp remove` cover common changes from a shell. See 【59†MCP commands】 for their options.
L198: ### Inspect or change a server
L199: 
L200: `/mcp` lists configured servers with their state, tool count, exposure, and configuration source. Servers that need attention appear first. Select a server to inspect its tools and connection details, reconnect, sign in or out, change exposure, or enable and disable it.
L201: Exposure and enabled-state changes are saved to the file that defines the server without replacing unrelated content. In a trusted project, "Enable in this project" and "Disable in this project" add a project override for a user-level server; later changes to that server are saved to the override. Disabled servers remain listed. Outside the interactive TUI, `/mcp` prints server status; `/mcp login <server>`, `/mcp logout <server>`, and `/mcp reconnect <server>` perform those actions directly.
L202: Shell commands work without a session: `pi mcp add`, `pi mcp remove`, `pi mcp list`, `pi mcp login`, and `pi mcp logout`. Shell commands do not load extensions.
L203: ### Diagnose connection problems
L204: 
L205: Run `pi mcp list` to connect to every enabled server and print its state, tools, and errors. It exits with status 1 when an entry is invalid or an enabled server is not connected. `/mcp` shows the full connection error and the tail of stderr from a failed stdio server.
L206: Pi reports configuration errors, failed connections, and required sign-ins once after startup. Server logging notifications are appended to `~/.pi/agent/mcp.log` as `<time> [<server>] <level> <logger>: <message>`. The file moves to `mcp.log.1` after it grows past 5 MB.
L207: Pi connects every enabled server in the background when a session starts. A server's tools appear once it connects; the `codemode` description does not list them, so it does not change when servers connect. The first prompt waits up to 10 seconds only for servers with `direct` tools, which must be declared in its request.
L208: Other servers are waited for when they are needed: a codemode script waits for the servers it names (`mcp__<server>`) and, when it calls `searchTools()` or reads `ALL_TOOLS`, for all of them; `tool_search` and the resource tools also wait for all of them. HTTP network errors and transient statuses (408, 429, and 5xx) are retried twice. A dropped connection is shown as disconnected and reconnects on the next call.
L209: When a server announces a changed tool list, new tools are added and withdrawn tools become unreachable.

Yes. **Find reference** would tell the agent exactly what’s missing for the solved phase, including its composition, structure, temperature, and pressure. The agent could query Materials Project using your preconfigured key through Rutile, search the web, download sources, and run Python to extract data or evaluate a published model. Click **Apply and rerun**, and Rutile attaches the Phase Data and refreshes the affected calculation using the saved equilibrium. There’s no manual data entry. If the evidence only supports density, elasticity stays unresolved.

The first version uses **Copy research task** to start the agent in Pi or Codex. Starting the agent directly from the button would be a follow-up integration.

# Alloy Studio reference research plan

Add **Find reference** to the Alloy Studio Inspector. Starting from a missing property on a solved phase, a connected agent searches for sources, downloads the files it needs, and writes and runs Python to extract or calculate a candidate value. Rutile checks the proposal and presents a Phase Data record for review. Applying the record reuses the saved equilibrium and refreshes the affected results.

This is a proposed feature. Alloy Studio already runs equilibrium, phase assignment, density, and tracer jobs through its local API. It can screen Materials Project records and attach condition-matched Phase Data. Those are the interfaces this work builds on. [Workflow API](../backend/src/rutile3/api/app.py#L271) · [Phase Data](processing.md#phase-assignment)

## Scope and architecture

Start with **density and elastic stiffness of a single solved solid phase** at one temperature and pressure. Cover disordered BCC, FCC, and HCP solutions where the source establishes the phase identity. A request for elasticity tracks whether bulk and shear moduli are both available. Grain size, strength, hardness, and processed-alloy properties follow their own models and are outside this work.

**The agent host runs the research.** Use a local MCP-capable host with web search, download, and Python capabilities. The host chooses queries, follows papers and supplements, and runs Python in a dedicated research directory. Codex is the first host to verify. Its existing sign-in and permissions apply to that setup.

**Rutile owns the scientific context and the graph.** Add a thin local stdio MCP adapter for the research tools. It calls narrowly scoped endpoints on the existing loopback FastAPI server, which in turn call ordinary Python services. The Inspector calls the same services through the browser API. Keep research state independent of the single active scientific job slot so that searching and downloading can run while a solver job executes. [Codex MCP configuration](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/extend/mcp?surface=cli) · [Rutile architecture](architecture.md)

Rutile needs no OpenAI API key for the Codex path. A future in-app runner could use OpenAI API or a local `llama-server` with a compatible tool-calling model and reuse the same request and proposal schemas. Both would need their own research execution and retrieval setup. No model provider is required for the scientific application itself. [Codex authentication](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/auth) · [llama.cpp function calling](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/function-calling.md)

## User workflow

1. **Start from the missing property.** Show **Find reference** next to a phase’s unavailable density or elasticity. Use the existing reason, such as a missing Hf density endmember, to select the search target. Display the phase label, actual atomic fractions, temperature, pressure, and what the external agent would receive. The user explicitly starts external research for that phase. Keep manual Phase Data entry available.
2. **Hand off via MCP.** Create a research request and a dedicated scratch directory. **Copy research task** gives the user the request ID, task objective, and instructions to paste into a connected agent host. The host calls Rutile through MCP to get the phase context. The copied text contains no credentials. Setup instructions explain how to open the research directory and connect the local MCP server.
3. **Collect evidence.** Check applicable local models and accepted references first. Query Materials Project for a crystal record when appropriate and use the host’s search for literature on the solution phase itself. Follow a DOI, report, or supplement to the value or equation. Use the host’s download tools to retain accessible source files in the research directory. Identify the table, figure, or equation that supplies each input. A host with search alone can still return cited leads.
4. **Extract or calculate.** Write a short Python script when a table, supplementary file, or published equation needs processing. Use the solved composition and stated conditions.
