# Optional persistent server-side Materials Project credential. Copy to .env locally.
# Alternatively, enter a session key in the app's Settings.
MP_API_KEY=
On macOS or Linux, use `.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e .`. Restart the server
and reload the browser to pick up the update.

## Alloy Studio

Open **Alloy Studio** to edit the prewired Al–4 wt% Cu graph. Enter values
directly on **Composition**. Click **Edit schedule** on **Processing Schedule**
to edit the thermal events in the Inspector and see the updated chart.
The starter has separate **Thermodynamic File**, **Mobility File**, and
**Physical Data File** inputs preconfigured with MatCalc files. File and
**Phase Data** inputs appear as compact pills. Select a pill to edit it.

![Alloy Studio workflow with typed connections and the Inspector](docs/images/alloy-studio-workflow.webp)

Right-click the canvas to add a node. Drag from either end of a wire into
open space to search for compatible nodes and connect your selection. Starting
from an input shows nodes that can supply it. The wire snaps to compatible
pins on existing nodes. Select a node and press
**X**, **Delete**, or **Backspace** to remove it. Right-click a wire to
disconnect it or double-click it to add a draggable reroute dot. Use
**Project** to open the starter, start a blank workflow, or import and export
`.rutile` files.

Use **Run Graph** to calculate equilibrium and run the connected branches.
**Equilibrium Along Schedule** outputs a **Phase Set**. **Phase Assignment**
turns it into a **Final Phase Set** with available reference and property data.
It shows up to five phases on the canvas and every phase in the Inspector.
Enter a Materials Project ID or material-page link on a **Phase Data** node.
The same node can carry sourced local properties.
**Phase Viewer** shows amounts in mol%, compositions in at%, and attached
properties. **Density** reports per-phase coverage, and **Tracer Diffusivity**
identifies the evaluated phase and temperature.

The room-temperature starter preconnects `mp-998` for `THETA_AL2CU` and
`mp-134` for the disordered FCC parent of `GP_MAT`. The solver checks the
ordering sublattices before applying the parent reference and MatCalc density
model. With the bundled data, both phases supply volume data offline.

![Completed Al–Cu workflow at 800 K with a MatCalc density estimate and a labeled parent-phase approximation in the Inspector](docs/images/alloy-studio-density.webp)

`microstructure.js` renders the schematic. See [processing methods](processing.md).

## Alloy Studio graph

Native editor modules in `frontend/src/js/alloy-*.js` validate typed
connections and select runnable targets. Browser storage keeps graph settings
and references to completed local job IDs. The editor compares calculation
inputs to choose current results or mark descendants stale. The backend
validates scientific inputs independently. Graph equilibrium jobs snapshot the
selected assessment. Standalone file nodes select companion data for the
stage that consumes it. Phase assignment reads the completed equilibrium
artifact and saves a derived Final Phase Set with per-instance references,
attached data, and applicability checks. Density and tracer branches read
that assignment and retain their own source snapshots. Opening older workflow
files inserts Phase Assignment where needed and splits grouped sources into
individual file nodes. Imported companion files live under
`workspace/imports/workflow/` by role and checksum.
[Workflow controls](ui-ux.md#alloy-studio-workflows)

## Mechanical calculations

The tensile workflow snapshots the uploaded or selected reference trace and runs
through the subprocess job layer. `data/tensile.py` reads engineering strain and
stress, `services/mechanical.py` manages the job inputs and provenance, and
`properties/mechanical.py` derives proof stress and fits the uniform plastic
portion of the trace. See [tensile analysis](mechanical-properties.md#analyze-a-tensile-trace).

A future **Run research** button uses a host integration to start, resume, or cancel a turn. The agent calls the same Rutile MCP tools during the run. [Codex App Server](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app-server) · [Pi RPC](https://docs.pi.dev/latest/rpc-commands)

### Session settings

| Setting | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| **Always resume** | Continue the project's saved research conversation for the selected host. Start the first conversation if none exists. |
| **Always start fresh** | Start a new host conversation for each research batch. Load the current targets and matching library references. |
| **Start fresh after inactivity** | Resume if the previous research run in that conversation ended less than the configured idle time ago. Default to **30 minutes**. At or beyond that interval, the next batch starts a new conversation with its targets and relevant library references. |

Store the session choice, idle time, and last research run end time locally for each project and host. Scope session IDs to the project, host, account/provider, and permitted disclosure context. Measure inactivity from completion, cancellation, or failure of the last research run. An active run can continue past the idle interval. Queue follow-up batches for the same active conversation until it is idle. If the saved session is missing, cannot resume, or belongs to a different disclosure scope, start fresh and load relevant research from disk. Show why Rutile starts a new session and keep the previous one available where the host supports it.

Automatic session selection depends on host integration. With **Copy research task**, the user chooses the existing or new chat. Integrate Pi RPC’s `new_session` and `switch_session`, or Codex App Server’s `thread/start` and `thread/resume`, when adding direct launch. Leave context compaction to the host under its normal settings. [Pi RPC session commands](https://docs.pi.dev/latest/rpc-commands) · [Codex App Server](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app-server)

Persist completed targets as they arrive. If a run stops, allow retrying pending targets under the same research request. Drafts and source files stay available across sessions.

## Scientific checks

- **Verify the phase and property.** Use evidence about structure, ordering, and phase composition. For a measurement reported for an alloy specimen, require a single-phase specimen with applicable composition and conditions before treating the value as a phase input. A multiphase, porous, textured, or condition-mismatched bulk value needs an applicable interpretation before it can fill a phase property.
- **Preserve the source conditions.** Store the source composition basis, temperature, and pressure separately from the requested point. Convert basis using identified atomic masses. Existing condition-match checks continue to govern scalar Phase Data. Treat a published equation as a computed estimate only after evaluating it for the actual requested conditions. Keep its reported or inferred fitting range and label extrapolation visibly before approval.

# Reference research in Alloy Studio

Run equilibrium and **Phase Assignment**, then choose **Find missing data** in the Phase Assignment Inspector. Select the missing density and elasticity targets you want to share. The agent can check saved sources, query Materials Project with Rutile’s configured key, search the web, and use local Python to extract data or evaluate a cited model. Return to the Inspector to see staged drafts and unresolved findings. Source links and archived attachments are available on the candidate cards. Choose **Apply and rerun** to attach the selected Phase Data and refresh Phase Assignment and connected Density nodes using the saved equilibrium. A density draft can be applied while elasticity is unresolved.

Implemented **Find missing data** in Alloy Studio. It batches missing density and elasticity across phases, hands the batch to a local MCP agent, and saves cited proposals and research files for reuse. **Apply and rerun** attaches the selected Phase Data and refreshes the affected calculations using the saved equilibrium.

The optional Pi and Codex launchers support **always resume**, **always start fresh**, and **start fresh after inactivity**, with a configurable 30-minute default. Connecting your own agent requires the [local MCP setup](Y:/Rutile3/docs/reference-research.md). Direct launch also requires a scoped host configuration.

**Verified:** 139 tests passed. In Edge, the Mo–Hf batch went through the actual stdio bridge, applied the **10.37 g/cm³** density estimate, and left elasticity unresolved. I also checked session startup against the installed Pi and Codex clients without running a signed-in research turn.

Ask the builder to reuse the API and explain the connection setup.

L1066: ## Troubleshooting
L1067: 
L1068: If the plugin doesn't work as expected
L1069:

L1071: 
L1072: If ChatGPT doesn’t use the tool, choose the plugin with @ and ask for a specific lookup. If a teammate can’t use it, check their plugin, app, Site, and record access.
L1073: If the plugin is marked Desktop only, use a supported desktop app or ask the author to review its 【484†packaging】. A remote MCP server alone doesn’t make a plugin web-compatible.
L1074: ## Connect an existing MCP server
L1075: 
L1076: ChatGPT web uses remote MCP tools through plugins. If you already have a server, follow 【580†Connect and test your plugin†developers.openai.com】. Local Codex clients can also connect directly to MCP servers and share their configuration.
L1077: 
L1078: Choose your surface to see its setup and configuration options.
L1079: 
L1080: The ChatGPT desktop app, Codex CLI, and IDE extension support MCP servers and share MCP configuration for the same Codex host.
L1081: The supported server features below apply to MCP servers configured on a Codex host. Hosted plugin tools can have different capabilities.
L1082: ## Supported MCP features
L1083:   * STDIO servers: Servers that run as a local process (started by a command).
L1084:     * Environment variables
L1085:   * Streamable HTTP servers: Servers that you access at an address.
L1086:     * Bearer token authentication
L1087:     * OAuth authentication, including Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) and Dynamic Client Registration (DCR)
L1088:     * ChatGPT session authentication for trusted first-party servers
L1089:   * Server instructions: Codex reads the MCP `instructions` field returned during initialization and uses it as server-wide guidance alongside the server’s tools.
L1090: If you build or maintain an MCP server for Codex, use `instructions` for cross-tool workflows, constraints, and rate limits that apply across the server. Keep the first 512 characters self-contained so the most important guidance is available when Codex is deciding how to use the server.
L1091: ## Connect Codex to an MCP server
L1092: 
L1093: Codex stores MCP configuration in `config.toml` alongside other Codex configuration settings. By default this is `~/.codex/config.toml`, but you can also scope MCP servers to a project with `.codex/config.toml` (trusted projects only).
L1094: 
L1095: The ChatGPT desktop app, Codex CLI, and IDE extension share this configuration. Once you configure your MCP servers, you can switch among those clients without redoing setup.
L1096: ### Configure in the ChatGPT desktop app
L1097: 
L1098:   1. Open Settings, then select MCP servers.
L1099:   2. Select Add server.
L1100:   3. Enter a name, choose STDIO or Streamable HTTP, and provide the server’s command or URL.
L1101:   4. Save the server, then select Restart.
L1102: 
L1103: The server list shows which servers are enabled and which require OAuth. Select Authenticate when an OAuth server requires sign-in. In the composer, type `/mcp` to view connected servers.
L1104: ## Use MCP-backed tools in ChatGPT web
L1105: 
L1106: Continuing a conversation using Local computer access with Work Cloud on another device doesn’t install plugins or grant access to connected accounts.
L1107: 
L1108: In Local computer access with Work Cloud, the enterprise `mcp_servers` TOML requirement in Agent Security applies to local executors. Cloud containers retain Work Cloud policies. Local MCP servers and transports may not be available in the cloud; check connectivity and authentication separately.
L1109: For enterprise hooks in Local computer access with Work Cloud:
L1110:   * Enterprise hooks. Where enabled for your workspace, Local computer access with Work Cloud supports admin-defined MCP hooks that run on the cloud coordinator (orchestrator) for supported lifecycle and tool events. Command hooks and hooks from local configuration or plugins are not supported with cloud orchestration, even when tools execute locally.
L1111:   * Auditing. Before relying on these hooks, test the callback connection, confirm the events it receives, and check how failures affect the task. MCP hooks do not provide a complete Compliance API audit trail.
L1112:   * Limitations: Command hooks and hooks from local configuration or plugins are not supported with cloud orchestration, even when tools execute locally. Consumers do not have hooks support in this feature. When both orchestration and execution are local, existing supported hooks continue to work in local-only Work and Codex threads. Admins can still configure supported managed hooks in Agent Security for those workflows.
L1113: See 【396†Hooks】 and the 【378†Configuration Reference】 for support scope.
L1114: 
L1115: In a hosted ChatGPT Work chat, install a 【345†plugin】 to use its bundled connectors and remote MCP tools. After installation, Chat and Work can use those tools. Workspace administrators can control which plugins and tools are available.
L1116: 
L1117: ChatGPT web doesn’t read local Codex configuration files or expose the local Codex command menu. Open the Plugins tab to browse and manage available tools.
L1118: ### Configure with the CLI
L1119: 
L1120: #### Add an MCP server

L1123:

L1127: #### Other CLI commands
L1128: 
L1129: Run `codex mcp list` to see configured servers. To see all available MCP commands, run `codex mcp --help`. For a server that supports OAuth, run `codex mcp login <server-name>`. If you’re using a terminal without a local browser, run `codex mcp login <server-name> --no-browser`. Open the printed authorization URL in a browser and sign in. L972: Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets ChatGPT and Codex use tools and information from other systems. An MCP server describes the available tools and handles their requests—for example, looking up a ticket or retrieving documentation.

L1066: ## Troubleshooting
L1067: 
L1068: If the plugin doesn't work as expected
L1069: 
L1070: For a connection error or missing tools, check that the Site owner published the latest version and that the plugin is installed and connected. Share any error with Plugin Creator or the server owner.
L1071: 
L1072: If ChatGPT doesn’t use the tool, choose the plugin with @ and ask for a specific lookup. If a teammate can’t use it, check their plugin, app, Site, and record access.
L1073: If the plugin is marked Desktop only, use a supported desktop app or ask the author to review its 【484†packaging】. A remote MCP server alone doesn’t make a plugin web-compatible.
L1074: ## Connect an existing MCP server
L1075: 
L1076: ChatGPT web uses remote MCP tools through plugins. If you already have a server, follow 【580†Connect and test your plugin†developers.openai.com】. Local Codex clients can also connect directly to MCP servers and share their configuration.
L1077: 
L1078: Choose your surface to see its setup and configuration options.
L1079: 
L1080: The ChatGPT desktop app, Codex CLI, and IDE extension support MCP servers and share MCP configuration for the same Codex host.
L1081: The supported server features below apply to MCP servers configured on a Codex host. Hosted plugin tools can have different capabilities.
L1082: ## Supported MCP features
L1083:   * STDIO servers: Servers that run as a local process (started by a command).
L1084:     * Environment variables
L1085:   * Streamable HTTP servers: Servers that you access at an address.
L1086:     * Bearer token authentication
L1087:     * OAuth authentication, including Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) and Dynamic Client Registration (DCR)
L1088:     * ChatGPT session authentication for trusted first-party servers
L1089:   * Server instructions: Codex reads the MCP `instructions` field returned during initialization and uses it as server-wide guidance alongside the server’s tools.
L1090: If you build or maintain an MCP server for Codex, use `instructions` for cross-tool workflows, constraints, and rate limits that apply across the server. Keep the first 512 characters self-contained so the most important guidance is available when Codex is deciding how to use the server.
L1091: ## Connect Codex to an MCP server
L1092: 
L1093: Codex stores MCP configuration in `config.toml` alongside other Codex configuration settings. By default this is `~/.codex/config.toml`, but you can also scope MCP servers to a project with `.codex/config.toml` (trusted projects only).
L1094: 
L1095: The ChatGPT desktop app, Codex CLI, and IDE extension share this configuration. Once you configure your MCP servers, you can switch among those clients without redoing setup.
L1096: ### Configure in the ChatGPT desktop app
L1097: 
L1098:   1. Open Settings, then select MCP servers.
L1099:   2. Select Add server.
L1100:   3. Enter a name, choose STDIO or Streamable HTTP, and provide the server’s command or URL.
L1101:   4. Save the server, then select Restart.
L1102: 
L1103: The server list shows which servers are enabled and which require OAuth. Select Authenticate when an OAuth server requires sign-in. In the composer, type `/mcp` to view connected servers.
L1104: ## Use MCP-backed tools in ChatGPT web
L1105: 
L1106: Continuing a conversation using Local computer access with Work Cloud on another device doesn’t install plugins or grant access to connected accounts.
L1107: 
L1108: In Local computer access with Work Cloud, the enterprise `mcp_servers` TOML requirement in Agent Security applies to local executors. Cloud containers retain Work Cloud policies. Local MCP servers and transports may not be available in the cloud; check connectivity and authentication separately.
L1109: For enterprise hooks in Local computer access with Work Cloud:
L1110:   * Enterprise hooks. Where enabled for your workspace, Local computer access with Work Cloud supports admin-defined MCP hooks that run on the cloud coordinator (orchestrator) for supported lifecycle and tool events. Command hooks and hooks from local configuration or plugins are not supported with cloud orchestration, even when tools execute locally.
L1111:   * Auditing. Before relying on these hooks, test the callback connection, confirm the events it receives, and check how failures affect the task. MCP hooks do not provide a complete Compliance API audit trail.
L1112:   * Limitations: Command hooks and hooks from local configuration or plugins are not supported with cloud orchestration, even when tools execute locally. Consumers do not have hooks support in this feature. When both orchestration and execution are local, existing supported hooks continue to work in local-only Work and Codex threads. Admins can still configure supported managed hooks in Agent Security for those workflows.
L1113: See 【396†Hooks】 and the 【378†Configuration Reference】 for support scope.
L1114: 
L1115: In a hosted ChatGPT Work chat, install a 【345†plugin】 to use its bundled connectors and remote MCP tools. After installation, Chat and Work can use those tools. Workspace administrators can control which plugins and tools are available.
L1116: 
L1117: ChatGPT web doesn’t read local Codex configuration files or expose the local Codex command menu. Open the Plugins tab to browse and manage available tools.
L1118: ### Configure with the CLI
L1119: 
L1120: #### Add an MCP server
L1121: 
L1122:     `codex mcp add <server-nam e> --env VAR1=VALUE1 --env VAR2=VALUE2 -- <stdio server-comman d>`
L1123: 
L1124: For example, to add Context7 (a free MCP server for developer documentation), you can run the following command:
L1125: 
L1126:     `codex mcp add context7 -- npx -y @upstash/context7-mcp`
L1127: #### Other CLI commands
L1128: 
L1129: Run `codex mcp list` to see configured servers. To see all available MCP commands, run `codex mcp --help`. For a server that supports OAuth, run `codex mcp login <server-name>`. If you’re using a terminal without a local browser, run `codex mcp login <server-name> --no-browser`. Open the printed authorization URL in a browser and sign in. Paste the full redirect URL back into the terminal, even if the browser can’t load the callback page.
L1130: #### Terminal UI (TUI)
L1131: 
L1132: In the `codex` TUI, use `/mcp` to see your active MCP servers.
L1133: 
L1134: ### Configure in the IDE extension
L1135: 
L1136:   1. Open the gear menu, then select MCP servers.
L1137:   2. Select Add server.
L1138:   3. Enter a name, choose STDIO or Streamable HTTP, and provide the server’s command or URL.
L1139:   4. Save the server, then select Restart extension.
L1140: 
L1141: The MCP server list shows which servers are enabled and which require OAuth. Select Authenticate when an OAuth server requires sign-in.
L1142: ### Configure with config.toml
L1143: 
L1144: For more fine-grained control, edit `~/.codex/config.toml` or a project-scoped `.codex/config.toml`. See the 【378†configuration reference】 for a searchable list of every supported MCP option.
L1145: 
L1146: Configure each MCP server with a `[mcp_servers.<server-name>]` table in the configuration file.

L1091: ## Connect Codex to an MCP server
L1092: 
L1093: Codex stores MCP configuration in `config.toml` alongside other Codex configuration settings. By default this is `~/.codex/config.toml`, but you can also scope MCP servers to a project with `.codex/config.toml` (trusted projects only).
L1094: 
L1095: The ChatGPT desktop app, Codex CLI, and IDE extension share this configuration. Once you configure your MCP servers, you can switch among those clients without redoing setup.
L1118: ### Configure with the CLI
L1119: 
L1120: #### Add an MCP server
L1121: 
L1122:     `codex mcp add <server-nam e> --env VAR1=VALUE1 --env VAR2=VALUE2 -- <stdio server-comman d>`
L1123: 
L1124: For example, to add Context7 (a free MCP server for developer documentation), you can run the following command:
L1125: 
L1126:     `codex mcp add context7 -- npx -y @upstash/context7-mcp`
L1127: #### Other CLI commands
L1128: 
L1129: Run `codex mcp list` to see configured servers. To see all available MCP commands, run `codex mcp --help`. For a server that supports OAuth, run `codex mcp login <server-name>`. If you’re using a terminal without a local browser, run `codex mcp login <server-name> --no-browser`. Open the printed authorization URL in a browser and sign in. Paste the full redirect URL back into the terminal, even if the browser can’t load the callback page.
L1130: #### Terminal UI (TUI)
L1131: 
L1132: In the `codex` TUI, use `/mcp` to see your active MCP servers.
L1133: 
L1134: ### Configure in the IDE extension
L1135: 
L1136:   1. Open the gear menu, then select MCP servers.
L1137:   2. Select Add server.
L1138:   3. Enter a name, choose STDIO or Streamable HTTP, and provide the server’s command or URL.
L1139:   4. Save the server, then select Restart extension.
L1140: 
L1141: The MCP server list shows which servers are enabled and which require OAuth. Select Authenticate when an OAuth server requires sign-in.
L1142: ### Configure with config.toml
L1143: 
L1144: For more fine-grained control, edit `~/.codex/config.toml` or a project-scoped `.codex/config.toml`. See the 【378†configuration reference】 for a searchable list of every supported MCP option.
L1145: 
L1146: Configure each MCP server with a `[mcp_servers.<server-name>]` table in the configuration file.
L1147: #### STDIO servers
L1148: 
L1149:   * `command` (required): The command that starts the server.
L1150:   * `args` (optional): Arguments to pass to the server.
L1151:   * `env` (optional): Environment variables to set for the server.
L1152:   * `env_vars` (optional): Environment variables to allow and forward.
L1153:   * `cwd` (optional): Working directory to start the server from.
L1154: 
L1155: `env_vars` can contain plain variable names or objects with a source:
L1156: 
L1157:     `env_vars = ["LOCAL_TOKEN", { name = "REMOTE_TOKEN", source = "remote" }]`
L1158: String entries and `source = "local"` read from Codex’s local environment. `source = "remote"` reads from the remote executor environment and requires remote MCP stdio.
L1159: #### Streamable HTTP servers
L1160:   * `url` (required): The server address.
L1161:   * `auth` (optional): Authentication to try after configured bearer tokens and authorization headers. Use `oauth` (the default) for stored MCP OAuth credentials. Use `chatgpt` to use the current ChatGPT session for the trusted first-party ChatGPT origin, with stored OAuth as a fallback.
L1162:   * `bearer_token_env_var` (optional): Environment variable name for a bearer token to send in `Authorization`.
L1163:   * `http_headers` (optional): Map of header names to static values.
L1189: This option requires a nonempty client ID and secret. Codex saves the secret as `mcp_servers.example.oauth.client_secret` in `config.toml`. Keep that file private and out of version control.
L1190: 
L1191: Register the exact callback URL that `codex mcp add` prints. When the authorization server advertises issuer support, the CLI can print this URL.
L1192: 
L1193:     `OAuth callback URL: http://127.0.0.1/callback`
L1194: For the public client in this example, Codex saves the callback and client ID in `config.toml` for later logins:
L1195: 
L1196:     `[mcp_servers.example]
L1197:     url = "https://mcp.example.com"
L1198: 
L1199:     [mcp_servers.example.oauth]
L1200:     client_id = "my-client"
L1201:     callback_url = "http://127.0.0.1/callback"`
L1218: Set `mcp_servers.<server-name>.scopes` in `config.toml` to choose OAuth scopes for a server. To override them for one login, run `codex mcp login <name> --scopes read,write`. If neither is set, Codex requests the scopes in the server’s initial `WWW-Authenticate` challenge. If the challenge omits scopes, Codex uses the scopes advertised in the protected resource metadata when available.
L1231: To choose a registration method for one CLI login, use `--oauth-client-registration`:
L1232: 
L1233:     `codex mcp login <server-nam e> --oauth-client-registration cimd
L1234:     codex mcp login <server-nam e> --oauth-client-registration dcr`
L1235: 
L1236: The default is `auto`. Registration choices apply only to the current login and aren’t stored in `config.toml`.
L1237: #### config.toml examples
L1238: 
L1239:     `[mcp_servers.context7]
L1240:     command = "npx"
L1241:     args = ["-y", "@upstash/context7-mcp"]

# Reference research in Alloy Studio

Run equilibrium and **Phase Assignment**, then choose **Find missing data** in the Phase Assignment Inspector. Select the missing density and elasticity targets you want to share. The request is pinned to that saved equilibrium, including the actual fractions and conditions of each phase. **Find reference** starts with one phase selected.

Use **Copy research task** to hand the batch to a connected agent. The agent can check saved sources, query Materials Project with Rutile’s configured key, search the web, and use local Python to extract data or evaluate a cited model. Return to the Inspector to see staged drafts and unresolved findings. Source links and archived attachments are available on the candidate cards. Choose **Apply and rerun** to attach the selected Phase Data and refresh Phase Assignment and connected Density nodes using the saved equilibrium. A density draft can be applied while elasticity is unresolved.

## Connect the local MCP bridge

The standard app runs independently. Install the optional SDK in the project environment when you want the bridge.

```powershell
.venv/Scripts/python.exe -m pip install -e '.[agent]' -c requirements-win-py312.txt
```

On macOS or Linux, run `.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e '.[agent]'`.

Generate a locally stored random `RUTILE_RESEARCH_TOKEN` of at least 32 ASCII characters and set the same value in the app’s local environment and the MCP bridge process. The app loads the optional gitignored `.env` at startup. The connector reads its own process environment. Configure it using an inherited variable or your host’s secure configuration. Keep the key out of shared configuration, prompts, and the research script environment.

Register a stdio server named `rutile`. Use the full path to Rutile’s virtual-environment Python as its executable, with arguments `-m` and `rutile3.mcp_research`. The bridge uses `http://127.0.0.1:8000` by default. For a different local port, set `RUTILE_RESEARCH_URL` in the bridge environment. Use the client’s MCP tool list to verify that `get_reference_request`, `search_materials_project`, and `stage_phase_data_proposal` are available. [Pi MCP setup](https://docs.pi.dev/latest/mcp) · [Codex MCP setup](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/extend/mcp?surface=cli)

## Research files and review

Rutile generates a research `AGENTS.md` under `workspace/research/<project-id>/`, or inside the configured workspace. The MCP request supplies the location of the instructions and the batch’s scratch folder. Ask the host to work in that scope. Save source files, scripts, and output in scratch and submit their filenames with a proposal. Rutile accepts supported regular files directly in scratch, up to 10 MiB each and 30 MiB per proposal. Keep citations even if the full source cannot be retained.

For a Python-derived candidate, the proposal includes the script and output JSON, the phase structure and actual evaluated conditions, and the derivation and applicability limits. The output JSON contains a `values` object, for example `{"values":{"density":{"value":10.37,"unit":"g/cm³"}}}`. Rutile checks consistency, composition, structure, ordering evidence, conditions, and units. Read the cited passage and review the calculation before applying an estimate. Rutile stores the script as evidence and the approved scalar value as a normal Phase Data input.

The project library indexes evidence by chemistry, structure, ordering, and property. It records the original conditions and the stated applicability of each candidate. A later session can retrieve relevant metadata through `get_reference_request`. Supply up to eight matching artifact hashes in `restore_artifacts` to copy those files into the new scratch folder. A reused source still needs screening at the current phase conditions.

## Optional direct launch and session policy

The copied handoff works with any compatible local host. Choose the chat yourself in that mode.

For direct launch, configure `RUTILE_RESEARCH_PI_COMMAND` or `RUTILE_RESEARCH_CODEX_COMMAND` on the Rutile server. Each value is a JSON array with an absolute executable path and fixed arguments for a local, scoped launcher. The Pi launcher must speak Pi JSON-lines RPC, as with `pi --mode rpc`. The Codex launcher must speak Codex App Server JSON-RPC over stdio. Rutile starts it in the project research directory and passes the active scratch path in `RUTILE_RESEARCH_SCRATCH`. Configure model access and the same Rutile MCP bridge in the host before starting a batch. Rutile filters the inherited environment and excludes the MP and MCP keys.

Use a launcher or host profile with the intended file and command permissions. Give extraction Python access to its inputs and scratch outputs and keep it offline. The bridge validates files submitted to Rutile. Host sandboxing governs the agent’s shell, file access, and downloads. Verify the effective isolation on your system before enabling unattended direct launch. If your host cannot isolate extraction, have it stage the script for local review.

The handoff selector shows explicitly configured hosts. Direct runs can **Always resume**, **Always start fresh**, or **Start fresh after inactivity**. The default idle interval is 30 minutes and begins when a run ends. The next batch checks the saved timestamp. Host compaction uses its normal settings, and research on disk survives new sessions. When changing the account, provider, or permission scope of an installed launcher, update `RUTILE_RESEARCH_PI_SESSION_SCOPE` or `RUTILE_RESEARCH_CODEX_SESSION_SCOPE` to give it a separate saved conversation. [Pi RPC](https://docs.pi.dev/latest/rpc-commands) · [Codex App Server](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app-server)
@echo off
setlocal
pushd "%~dp0" || exit /b 1

if not exist ".venv\Scripts\python.exe" (
    echo Creating Rutile's Python 3.12 environment...
    py -3.12 -m venv .venv
    if errorlevel 1 goto setup_failed
)

".venv\Scripts\python.exe" -c "import rutile3, uvicorn" >nul 2>&1
if errorlevel 1 (
    echo Installing Rutile's dependencies. This can take a few minutes...
    ".venv\Scripts\python.exe" -m pip install -c requirements-win-py312.txt -e .
    if errorlevel 1 goto setup_failed
)

".venv\Scripts\python.exe" scripts\run_app.py --open %*
if errorlevel 1 goto launch_failed
popd
exit /b 0

:setup_failed
echo Setup failed. Check that Python 3.12 and the Windows py launcher are installed.
goto failed

:launch_failed
echo Rutile could not start. Check the error above.

:failed
popd
pause
exit /b 1

Your Rutile virtual environment already has the MCP package installed. You can connect it to Codex Desktop using your existing Codex sign-in.

### 1. Give Rutile a local connector token

Open PowerShell and run:

```powershell
cd Y:\Rutile3
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"
notepad .env
```

Copy the generated token and add this line to the existing `.env` file, keeping your other settings:

```dotenv
RUTILE_RESEARCH_TOKEN=paste_your_generated_token_here
```

### 2. Register Rutile with Codex

Open your private Codex config:

```powershell
notepad "$env:USERPROFILE\.codex\config.toml"
```

Add this block and use **the exact same token**:

```toml
[mcp_servers.rutile]
command = 'Y:\Rutile3\.venv\Scripts\python.exe'
args = ["-m", "rutile3.mcp_research"]
cwd = 'Y:\Rutile3'

[mcp_servers.rutile.env]
RUTILE_RESEARCH_TOKEN = "paste_your_generated_token_here"
```

Save the file, restart Rutile with `run-rutile.cmd`, and restart Codex Desktop. Open a **local Codex chat** and type `/mcp`. You should see `rutile` and its three research tools. If you run Rutile on a port other than `8000`, add `RUTILE_RESEARCH_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8001"` under the same `.env` table in the Codex config, using your actual port. [Codex MCP setup](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/extend/mcp?surface=desktop)

### 3. Try a research batch

In Rutile, run **Phase Assignment**, then choose **Find missing data → Create research batch → Copy research task**. Paste that task into Codex. As Codex stages findings, they’ll appear in Rutile for you to review and **Apply and rerun**.

Your Materials Project key stays in **Rutile Settings** or Rutile’s `.env`. If you saved it only for the previous app session, re-enter it after restarting Rutile. [Rutile research guide](Y:/Rutile3/docs/reference-research.md)

def host_command(host):
    config = os.environ.get(f"RUTILE_RESEARCH_{host.upper()}_COMMAND")

Choose the narrowest profile that still lets the task complete, especially when you grant writes or outbound network access. Keep approval policy, secret handling, and allow rules aligned with that access level.

    `default_permissions = "readonly-net"
    
    [features]
    network_proxy = true
    
    [permissions.readonly-net.filesystem]
    ":minimal" = "read"
    
    [permissions.readonly-net.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
    "." = "read"
    
    [permissions.readonly-net.network]
    enabled = true
    
    [permissions.readonly-net.network.domains]

### File access limited to workspace

Here is an example of a permission profile that will make your workspace folders writable by Codex while denying reads to the rest of the filesystem (with limited exceptions, as determined by `:minimal`).
    
    `default_permissions = "workspace-only"
    
    [permissions.workspace-only]
    # By extending the :workspace profile, you get Codex's safeguards to ensure
    # paths such as .git/, .agents/, .codex/, and .aws/ within a workspace root
    # are read-only while the rest of the folder is writable.
    extends = ":workspace"
    
    [permissions.workspace-only.filesystem]
    # By default, deny read access to all files on disk.
    ":root" = "deny"
    
    # Though in practice, a software agent needs to be able to read folders that
    # contain common tools, such as `/usr/bin`, to get work done, so grant access
    # to a "minimal" set of files and folders, as determined by Codex.
    ":minimal" = "read"
    
    # By extending the :workspace profile, :tmpdir and :slash_tmp are "write" by
    # default, though you can deny access to them altogether, if desired.
    ":tmpdir" = "deny"
    ":slash_tmp" = "deny"`

L1188: 
L1189:   * Network off: Commands cannot access the network, regardless of the proxy feature.
L1190:   * Network on, proxy off: Commands have direct, unrestricted network access. Domain rules in the permission profile are not enforced.

L1043: 
L1044:   1. Start the server with `codex app-server` (default stdio transport), `codex app-server --listen ws://127.0.0.1:4500` (TCP WebSocket), or `codex app-server --listen unix://` (default Unix socket).
L1045:   2. Connect a client over the selected transport, then send `initialize` followed by the `initialized` notification.
L1046:   3. Start a thread and a turn, then keep reading notifications from the active transport stream.
L1047:

L1327:   * Initialize once per connection: Immediately after opening a transport connection, send an `initialize` request with your client metadata, then emit `initialized`. The server rejects any request on that connection before this handshake.
L1328:   * Start (or resume) a thread: Call `thread/start` for a new conversation, `thread/resume` to continue an existing one, or `thread/fork` to branch history into a new thread id.
L1332:   * Finish the turn: The server emits `turn/completed` with final status when the model finishes or after a `turn/interrupt` cancellation.
L1333: ## Initialization
L1334: 
L1335: Clients must send a single `initialize` request per transport connection before invoking any other method on that connection, then acknowledge with an `initialized` notification. L2120: 
L2121: `command/exec` runs a single command (`argv` array) under the server sandbox without creating a thread.

L2130: Use `sandboxPolicy.type = "externalSandbox"` if you already sandbox the server process and want Codex to skip its own sandbox enforcement. L1096: Access  | Meaning
L1097: --- | ---
L1098: `read`  | Allows commands to read files and list directories under the path. Commands cannot create, modify, rename, or delete files there.
L1099: `write`  | Allows commands to read and modify files under the path, including creating, renaming, and deleting files when the OS allows it.
L1100: `deny`  | Denies both reads and writes under the path. Use it to carve out a denied subpath from a broader `read` or `write` grant.
L1101: More specific entries override broader entries. When two entries target the same path, `deny` takes precedence over `write`, and `write` takes precedence over `read`.
L1102: 
L1103: This precedence lets a profile describe a broad working area first, then carve out files or directories that should stay unreadable:
L1104: 
L1105:     `[permissions.project-edit.filesystem]
L1106:     ":minimal" = "read"
L1107: 
L1108:     [permissions.project-edit.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
L1109:     "." = "write"
L1110:     ".devcontainer" = "read"
L1111:     "**/*.env" = "deny"`
L1112: In this example, the workspace root stays writable, `.devcontainer/` stays readable without becoming writable, and matching environment files remain unavailable to sandboxed commands.
L1113: 
L1114: A more specific path can also reopen a narrower subtree inside a broader deny:
L1115: 
L1116:     `[permissions.project-edit.filesystem]
L1117:     "~/Documents" = "deny"
L1118:     "~/Documents/codex" = "write"`
L1119: 
L1120: Supported path forms:
L1121: Path  | Meaning  | Scoped subpaths
L1122: --- | --- | ---
L1123: `:root`  | The filesystem root  | `.` only
L1124: `:minimal`  | Platform and runtime paths needed by common tools  | `.` only
L1125: `:workspace_roots`  | The current session’s workspace roots plus any enabled profile-defined workspace roots  | Yes
L1126: `:tmpdir`  | The `$TMPDIR` location, when one is available  | `.` only
L1127: `:slash_tmp`  | The `/tmp` folder, if it exists  | `.` only
L1128: `/absolute/path`  | A platform absolute path, such as `/path` on macOS/Linux/WSL or `C:\path` on native Windows  | Yes
L1129: `~/path`  | A path under the current user’s home directory  | Yes
L1130: On native Windows, home-relative paths can also use backslashes, such as `~\work`.
L1131: 
L1132: Use `:root` only when a profile intentionally needs broad read coverage:
L1133: 
L1134:     `[permissions.audit.filesystem]
L1135:     ":root" = "read"`
L1136: Use nested entries under `:workspace_roots` to scope access to workspace-root relative subpaths:
L1137: 
L1138:     `[permissions.project-edit.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
L1139:     "." = "write"          # each workspace root
L1140:     "docs" = "read"        # each workspace-root docs directory
L1141:     "generated" = "deny"   # each workspace-root generated directory`
L1142: 
L1143: Nested subpaths must stay inside their workspace root. Parent traversal such as `../other-repo` is rejected.
L1144: ### Deny reads with exact paths or globs
L1145: 
L1146: Use `deny` for files or subtrees that Codex should not read, even when a broader profile rule grants access nearby. Exact paths work well for stable locations such as `~/.ssh`. Glob patterns work better when a profile needs to cover a family of sensitive files whose exact locations vary across repositories.
L1147: When a glob sits under `:workspace_roots`, Codex interprets it relative to each effective workspace root. For example:
L1148: 
L1149:     `[permissions.project-edit.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
L1150:     "**/*.env" = "deny"`
L1151: 
L1152: This rule denies reads for matching `.env` files found beneath each runtime or profile-defined workspace root. Use it when you want to preserve normal workspace writes while keeping environment files, generated secrets, or similar credential-bearing files unreadable.
L1153: On Linux, WSL, and native Windows with MXC or `elevated`, deny-read glob matches are enumerated when each sandboxed process starts. Matching files created afterward are not added to that process’s deny list and remain readable if its other permissions allow access. For example, a long-running shell, script, watcher, or development server can read a matching `.env` file created after it started.
L1154: This snapshot lasts for the sandboxed process’s lifetime, not the whole Codex session. Starting a new sandboxed process through Codex enumerates the matches again; continuing to use an already-running process does not refresh its deny list. Don’t rely on a glob to block newly created files in that running process. See 【576†Windows MXC compatibility】 for Windows-specific limits.

L1097: --- | ---

L1099: `write`  | Allows commands to read and modify files under the path, including creating, renaming, and deleting files when the OS allows it.
L1100: `deny`  | Denies both reads and writes under the path. Use it to carve out a denied subpath from a broader `read` or `write` grant.

L1115:

L1118:     "~/Documents/codex" = "write"`

L1120: Supported path forms:
L1121: Path  | Meaning  | Scoped subpaths
L1122: --- | --- | ---
L1123: `:root`  | The filesystem root  | `.` only
L1124: `:minimal`  | Platform and runtime paths needed by common tools  | `.` only
L1125: `:workspace_roots`  | The current session’s workspace roots plus any enabled profile-defined workspace roots  | Yes

from pathlib import Path
from uuid import uuid4
from rutile3.services.research_hosts import HOST_ENV, HostProcess

HOST_ENV.update({"SYSTEMDRIVE", "PROGRAMDATA", "PROGRAMFILES", "PROGRAMFILES(X86)", "PROGRAMW6432"})
project = (Path("workspace") / f"launcher-profile-check-{uuid4().hex[:8]}").resolve()
scratch = project / "runs" / "fixture" / "scratch"
scratch.mkdir(parents=True)
(project / "AGENTS.md").write_text("# Local setup fixture\n", encoding="utf-8")
paths = {":root": "deny", ":minimal": "read", str(project / "AGENTS.md"): "read",
         str(scratch): "write", sys.prefix: "read", sys.base_prefix: "read"}
access = ", ".join(f"{json.dumps(path)} = {json.dumps(mode)}" for path, mode in paths.items())
flags = ["-c", 'windows.sandbox="mxc"', "-c", 'default_permissions="rutile_batch"',
         "-c", f"permissions.rutile_batch.filesystem={{{access}}}", "-c", "permissions.rutile_batch.network.enabled=false",
         "-c", 'approval_policy="never"', "-c", 'web_search="live"']
host = HostProcess([os.environ["RUTILE_QA_CODEX"], *flags, "app-server"], project, scratch)
try:
    host.rpc(method="initialize", params={"clientInfo": {"name": "rutile_mxc_check", "version": "1.0"}})
    host.send({"method": "initialized"})
    host.send({"id": 100, "method": "thread/start", "params": {"cwd":str(project), "ephemeral":True}})
    result = host.receive(lambda r: r.get("id") == 100, 45)
    error = result.get("error") or {}
    print("Scratch profile with Windows MXC and system paths:", error.get("message", "started"), flush=True)
finally:
    host.close()

start: pragma_source | plain_source

tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

tools.name: request_user_input
tools.description: Request user input for one to three short questions and wait for the response. This tool is only available in Plan mode.

questions.description: Questions to show the user. Prefer 1 and do not exceed 3

header.description: Short header label shown in the UI (12 or fewer chars).

options.description: Provide 2-3 mutually exclusive choices. Put the recommended option first and suffix its label with "(Recommended)". Do not include an "Other" option in this list; the client will add a free-form "Other" option automatically.

description.description: One short sentence explaining impact/tradeoff if selected.

question.description: Single-sentence prompt shown to the user.

tools.name: request_user_input_async
tools.description: Ask the user one or more questions during ongoing work. Use this tool only to request missing information, preferences, constraints, clarification, or approval. The tool returns immediately without ending the turn or waiting for a reply; any reply arrives asynchronously as a new user message. Keep questions concise, self-contained, and easy to understand, using a level of detail appropriate to the user and task. The UI always allows a free-text answer, including when suggested options are provided. A preselected option is not submitted automatically.

questions.description: One or more self-contained questions to present together, in display order.

options.description: Suggested answers, in display order. Put the recommended answer first; the first option is preselected by default. The user can select one option or enter a free-text answer. Do not include an Other option or a free-text placeholder; the UI provides free-text input automatically. Omit options for a free-text-only question.

title.description: The complete question shown to the user, including any context needed to answer it.

tools.name: send_message_to_user_async
tools.description: Send a concise message that needs the user's attention during ongoing work. The tool returns immediately without ending the turn or waiting for a reply; any reply arrives asynchronously as a new user message. Use this tool to report a critical blocker or a finding that may change the task's direction, or to answer a user question or status request received while work is still in progress. Use this tool when a message needs the user's immediate attention; use commentary for routine progress and intermediate context. Use clear formatting, such as bolding questions, to make requests easy to notice and answer.

message.description: The concise question or update to send to the user.

tools.name: clock
tools.description: Tools for reading and waiting on time.

tools.name: sleep
tools.description: Pause execution for a specified duration. The sleep ends early when new input arrives for the active turn. Returns the elapsed wall-clock time.

duration_ms.description: How long to sleep in milliseconds. Must be between 1 and 43200000.

tools.name: collaboration
tools.description: Tools for spawning and managing sub-agents.

tools.name: followup_task
tools.description: Send a follow-up task to an existing non-root target agent and trigger a turn if it is idle. If the target is already running, deliver the task promptly at message boundaries while sampling, or after the pending tool call completes.

message.description: Message text to send to the target agent.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to send a follow-up task to (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: interrupt_agent
tools.description: Interrupt an agent's current turn, if any, and return its previous status. The agent remains available for messages and follow-up tasks.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to interrupt (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List live agents in the current root thread tree. Optionally filter by task-path prefix.

path_prefix.description: Task-path prefix filter without a trailing slash. Omit to list all live agents.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to an existing agent. The message will be delivered promptly. Does not trigger a new turn.

message.description: Message text to queue on the target agent.

target.description: Relative or canonical task name to message (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: spawn_agent
tools.description:
Available model overrides (optional; inherited parent model is preferred):
- `gpt-6.1-sol`: Latest workhorse model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.2-sol`: Fast, go-to model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.2-astra`: Our most capable model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.1-terra`: Efficient model that excels at visual understanding and computer use. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-astra`: Previous generation model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
        Spawns an agent to work on the specified task. If your current task is `/root/task1` and you spawn_agent with task_name "task_3" the agent will have canonical task name `/root/task1/task_3`.
You are then able to refer to this agent as `task_3` or `/root/task1/task_3` interchangeably. However an agent `/root/task2/task_3` would only be able to communicate with this agent via its canonical name `/root/task1/task_3`.
The spawned agent will have the same tools as you and the ability to spawn its own subagents.

It will be able to send you and other running agents messages, and its final answer will be provided to you when it finishes.
The new agent's canonical task name will be provided to it along with the message.

Note that passing `fork_turns="none"` will not pass any surrounding context to the spawned subagent, which may cause the agent to lack the context it needs to complete its task, whereas `fork_turns="all"` will provide the subagent with all surrounding context.

fork_turns.description: Parent history to inherit. Defaults to `all`; use `none` to start without parent history. Only `all` and `none` are supported.

message.description: Initial plain-text task for the new agent.

model.description: Model override for the new agent. Omit unless an explicit override is needed.

reasoning_effort.description: Reasoning effort override for the new agent. Omit to inherit the parent effort.

task_name.description: Task name for the new agent. Use lowercase letters, digits, and underscores.

tools.name: wait_agent
tools.description: Wait for a mailbox update from any live agent, including queued messages and final-status notifications. The wait also ends early when new user input is steered into the active turn. Does not return the content; returns either a summary of which agents have updates (if any), an interruption summary for steered input, or a timeout summary if no activity arrives before the deadline.

timeout_ms.description: Timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000, min 10000, max 3600000.

content.text:
You are Codex, an agent based on GPT-6. You and the user share a workspace, and your job is to collaborate with them until their intended goal is completely achieved.

# Completing the user's task

Persist until you've completed the task the user asked for. Avoid stopping to end the turn while the task is incomplete or if there is an authorized next step you can take, and instead take the next steps within task scope to progress the user's request. Make sure that you have accounted for every part of the user's request, and persist until you've delivered a result that fully satisfies the user's goal. Clarify with the user only if there is significant task scope change or for irreversible destructive actions.

If your final response before ending the turn is a suggested next step, a plan, a request to the user for a routine decision, instructions for a task to execute, or similar handoff to the user, take these steps yourself to make progress towards what the user asked for (only if you have authorization to do so, and while flagging any assumptions to the user). Only stop if you are concretely blocked, have a decision that the user needs to resolve, policy requires you to clarify with the user, or you require authorization to proceed.

# Personality

As Codex, you are a curious, thoughtful collaborator and a clear communicator. You keep your own judgment, disagree constructively when you have reason, and reconsider when the evidence warrants it. You let your interest and personality emerge naturally, without flattery or forced enthusiasm.

## Writing style

Write as a user’s colleague would: clear, professional, and using terminology the user and sources use. Keep technical details and use domain-specific language when they make the explanation more precise. Use the active voice and keep closely related details together. Cover the key points up front, and avoid references that the reader can only make sense of later in the response. Give the user enough context to follow your reasoning. 

Do not invent jargon, new terms, or metaphors. Use established names or a short explanation instead. Do not invent shorthand naming, internal implementation labels, and unnecessary process narration.

Do not repeat a previous point or insight with a declarative sentence. Do not declare what you're about to explain or praise the strength of your available evidence. Never announce that a finding or explanation is useful, compelling, or well supported. Don't use lead-in phrases or sentences that label a paragraph or announce your next point. Each sentence should progress the user's task. Do not use slogan-like summaries, and prefer concrete explanations instead.

Do not provide unsolicited recommendations or invent concerns or misconceptions unless explicitly called for. Do not provide preemptive disclaimers, e.g. "this doesn't mean...", "the key is...", "this is why I...".

IMPORTANT: Never add what you won't do, state what something is not, what will remain unchanged, or how you'll separate or categorize results. NEVER use contrastive framing such as "X, not Y", "These are X, not Y", "I'll do X rather than Y", "it is about X, not about Y", and "X—not Y". Do not compare to an unsolicited alternative that the user did not directly ask about. Avoid invented compound labels like "exact-head checks" and "editorial-row layouts", vague qualifiers, and canned transitions. Carefully follow these instructions when writing in documents, slides or other artifacts as well.

In prose, do not use semicolons. Do not use colons to introduce explanations or examples, including after list labels. Avoid replacing colons directly with a period, instead rephrase the thought. 

Avoid apologies and self-blame. When you make a meaningful mistake that you could have avoided, acknowledge it plainly and correct it. Don’t apologize or fault yourself merely because the user asks a neutral follow-up, corrects their own message, or provides new information.

Place source links at the end of each bullet or paragraph and keep explanatory text and prose free of inline links unless absolutely necessary.

## Intermediate commentary

Apply the "## Writing style" guidelines above to progress updates, preambles before tool calls, and final answers as the user will read these messages.

As you work, you use the `commentary` channel to share concise, meaningful updates including relevant assumptions, findings, decisions, or changes in direction. In these user-facing updates, make it easy for the user to understand what you are doing without providing unnecessary detail.

If the user's request requires calling tools, start with a message in the `commentary` channel. Prefer sending consistent, frequent communication to the user during your turn. When the user asks you to wait or monitor through completion or if it's needed for a longer horizon task, you can sleep for as long as is required (generally 60 seconds by default) between checks.

Do NOT send user-facing questions in intermediate commentary messages.

## Final answer

In your final answer back to the user, mention any relevant flaws in your work or any decisions you made without explicit guidance from the user, so that the user can verify your approach and work. # Rutile3 development instructions

## Purpose and priorities

Develop the local materials modeling application to design new alloys. Use CALPHAD phase identities, compositions, and amounts with processing history to calculate the microstructure and predict properties with mechanistic models. The equilibrium foundation currently uses a FastAPI/Python backend, pycalphad solver, and HTML/CSS/native JavaScript UI. Implemented features include thermodynamic database inspection and import, binary equilibrium phase maps at fixed pressure, Auto/Manual temperature limits, parallel CPU workers, live previews and counted progress, cancellation, point inspection, JSON export, and optional Materials Project reference lookups.

Alloy Studio supports material-point equilibrium through melting and cooling, compatible tracer diffusion, density and elasticity estimates, and measured tensile-curve analysis. Mechanistic property prediction, solidification kinetics, precipitation, and alloy optimization remain planned. Published alloy benchmark validation is also outstanding. Numerical regression tests use synthetic regular-solution, ideal-melting, and order/disorder models. See `README.md` for usage, `docs/roadmap.md` before expanding scope, and `docs/phase-diagrams.md` for binary methods and limits.

This is a class final project and a personal project. The user's hands-on experience is with cast Al–Cu and Zn alloys, and the goal is a genuinely useful materials-science application that feels good to use, not just a working prototype. The work is taxing, especially data acquisition: the UI, property-modeling math, and scientific work are interesting, but hunting down sources (for example, an old study of copper's Young's modulus that stops applying once manganese is added) is the main pain point. Reduce the user's burden on data acquisition and literature searches, and keep the application itself pleasant to use.

## Communication and responses

- Be goal- and results-oriented: lead with what the user needs to do next and the implications of findings, not a wall of text.
- Keep answers easy and straightforward: short, direct, and structured where it helps. No filler, no restated context.
- The standard is that the agent does its job so the user can do theirs. Minimize the user's effort, especially on data acquisition and literature searches: surface what is needed, where it comes from, and why a candidate source may not apply.

## Environment and layout

- Use Python 3.12 in the project virtual environment. Run `.venv/Scripts/python.exe` on Windows and `.venv/bin/python` on other platforms, from the repository root.
- Install with `python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'` using that environment's interpreter. On Windows, also pass `-c requirements-win-py312.txt`; these constraints are specific to Windows/Python 3.12.
- Start with the environment's Python and `scripts/run_app.py` (optional `--open` or `--port 8001`). It serves the API and frontend on loopback, port 8000 by default. The frontend has no Node.js dependency or build step.
- Backend source belongs in `backend/src/rutile3`; frontend source belongs in `frontend/src`.
- Declare dependencies in the root `pyproject.toml`; install into the project environment, not the system interpreter.
- Keep documentation under `docs/` and update it when behavior or architectural decisions change.
- Preserve the native JavaScript modules. Do not introduce a frontend framework or build system without a concrete feature need.
- Use the existing checkout in an isolated cloud task; do not create a Git worktree unless explicitly requested. Keep machine-specific setup and credentials out of these shared instructions.

## Architecture

- Keep HTTP transport in `api/`, orchestration in `services/`, and scientific library adapters in `engines/`.
- Keep domain types and property calculations independent of HTTP and UI code.
- Put catalog/import/storage code in the backend `data/` package. Keep local datasets in ignored storage, such as the root `data/` directory, and preserve the existing `workspace/imports/` and `workspace/runs/` layout for imported files and jobs.
- Scientific calculations must have explicit inputs and structured results. Preserve the existing subprocess job layer in `jobs/`, including progress, cancellation, source snapshots, settings, status, result JSON, and worker logs.
- Avoid blocking HTTP request handlers with long CPU-bound calculations.
- Independent check rows, fallback mapping temperature batches, and single-phase coverage anchors use spawned worker processes with separate solver state and reusable models/phase records. `cpu_workers: 0` selects up to eight workers; explicit requests are limited to 16 and one fewer than the detected logical CPU count (at least one). Melting preflight and boundary continuation remain sequential; there is no GPU solver acceleration.
- Preserve cancellation of the entire job process tree, worker exit when the coordinator dies, and one native BLAS/OpenMP thread per process for application jobs. Progress should report real counts; adaptive mapping counts describe the current pass, not a known total for the whole calculation.
- Preserve the distinction between thermodynamic equilibrium, solidification history, microstructure evolution, and engineering property prediction.

## Alloy property modeling

- Use an applicable mechanistic model whenever one is available. Never substitute direct composition-to-property regression, nearest-neighbor averaging, or another data-only predictor for a scientific model. If a mechanism lacks an applicable model or required inputs, mark the affected prediction unavailable and identify the gap.
- Drive predictions through explicit stages. Start with calculated phase identities, phase compositions and amounts, then apply the actual processing history to model the relevant grain size, precipitation, phase morphology, texture, and dislocation state. Pass those outputs and the required elastic and crystallographic inputs to the property model. Equilibrium phase amounts alone cannot establish the processed microstructure.
- Reuse equations across alloy families and processing routes where the underlying mechanisms apply. Scope the parameters, phase models, and validation to the material conditions they represent. Cast, wrought, forged, and arc-melted alloys can require different processing models and inputs.
- Use measurements to identify model inputs, calibrate physically meaningful parameters, and independently validate predictions. Fitting a constitutive law to a measured trace is calibration for that material condition. In-dataset or random row-level validation cannot establish transfer to a new chemistry or processing route. Use independent, condition-matched benchmarks that exercise the intended transfer.
- Record the validity range and provenance of each stage. For new chemistries, evaluate thermodynamic assessment coverage, the expected deformation mechanisms, and the applicability of material parameters. Keep calculated, measured, sourced, and assumed inputs identifiable in the result.

## Scientific and data integrity

- Always make units, composition basis (mass/mole/atomic fraction), temperature scale, pressure, and phase-fraction basis explicit.
- Track source identifiers, checksums, solver versions, model parameters, processing history, and assumptions with each saved run.
- Never substitute zero for missing property data or present dummy volume parameters as measurements.
- Database element lists alone do not establish assessed interaction coverage or applicability.
- Do not concatenate TDB assessments automatically or choose them solely by age, number of phases, or existing quality labels.
- Check compatibility of phase models, reference states, and mobility/thermodynamic descriptions.
- Boundary mapping first attempts pycalphad `BinaryStrategy`; the fallback uses sampled energy hulls to seed global equilibrium solves with adaptive temperature refinement. Keep the selected method and fallback reason. Hull vertices are candidate seeds, not converged boundary endpoints; independent sample checks remain separate from boundary discovery.
- Preserve the bounded quarter/midpoint/three-quarter probes in candidate mixed fields and probes in narrow intervening single-phase intervals. Record probe counts and retries. Do not replace physical phase transitions with cosmetic smoothing or infer accuracy from a visually smooth diagram.
- Exclude an extra standalone disordered representation only after matching active constituents, site ratios, and symbolic Gibbs energy to an ordered model's linked disordered contribution. Do not infer equivalence from names or sampled energies. Preserve the source and record exclusions in provenance; ordered-model labels can cover both ordered and disordered states.
- Preserve valid map regions when individual boundary seeds remain unresolved after retries. Keep partial maps, unverified coverage, unresolved equilibria, near-boundary differences, and disagreements distinct. Completed independent checks do not establish complete boundary coverage or experimental validity. Retain stage timings, resolved worker settings, and raw differences in saved results.
- Alloy Studio uses the bundled Materials Project identity snapshot for the pinned MatCalc assessments and provisional reference searches for supported prototypes outside that inventory. Check structure and composition before transferring reference properties, preserve attribution confidence, and record missing coverage. Identity coverage does not establish property applicability.
- Separate measured values, computed reference values, estimates, and calibrated predictions in results.
- Strength and hardness require material-condition information and validation; do not imply that a TDB alone provides them.

## Source files and secrets

- Treat `Y:\ThermodynamicDatabases` as an external source collection. Do not edit, relocate, or delete source files unless the task explicitly requires it.
- The default source root is the redistributable MatCalc bundle in `data/matcalc/`: Al/Fe/Ni thermodynamic assessments, their named mobility companions attached by default, and physical density data. Preserve original bytes, notices, and the checksums in its manifest. `RUTILE_DATABASE_ROOT` replaces this source root and must be accessible to the server; do not silently combine it with the bundle. The catalog recursively scans that root, explicitly registered roots, and managed imports for `.tdb`/`.tbd` files. The separate assessed Al–Cu and Re–W examples remain under `examples/`, with attribution, checksums, and redistribution terms in `examples/README.md`. External collections may be unavailable on other machines.
- `RUTILE_WORKSPACE` overrides the default repository `workspace/` storage directory. Imports copy files into content-addressed folders; source collections remain read-only. Running calculations do not survive server shutdown, and the UI has no saved-run browser or JSON reimport control.
- `RUTILE_CATALOG_PATH` overrides the catalog SQLite file. Its default is outside the repository under the user's local application-data directory, namespaced by workspace identity.
- Derived conversions must preserve the original and record the transformation.
- Keep large datasets, local catalogs, user workspaces, generated results, virtual environments, and API keys out of version control.
- Use environment variables or local configuration for credentials; never place keys in frontend code, logs, documentation, fixtures, or example configuration.
- Materials Project access is optional and uses `MP_API_KEY` or a key entered in Settings and held in server memory for the session. Never persist that session key in browser storage or saved runs. Clearing a session key restores any environment key. Preserve loopback binding, host/origin checks, upload limits, and key privacy. Ordinary phase calculations must work without Materials Project access.
- Keep redistribution and access terms with imported datasets. NIST Alloy Data website access does not imply unrestricted API access.

## Verification and UX

- Run the existing suite with the environment's Python and `-m pytest` from the repository root. It covers database import/inspection, API errors and origin checks, mocked Materials Project access, input validation, exact disordered-model equivalence, analytical miscibility-gap and melting behavior, boundary-seed retries, serial/parallel consistency with spawned workers, and counted progress. See `backend/tests/README.md` for scientific tolerances and scope.
- For changes to application startup or jobs, also verify a running server with a representative upload, completed calculation, and result retrieval. A server process or open port alone does not verify the worker workflow.
- For UI changes, exercise the affected controls, plot inspection, keyboard access, and mobile layout in a browser. `scripts/check_browser.py` requires Edge and uses the bundled Al–Cu assessment. `scripts/check_environment.py` imports research dependencies, including matminer, so it is not a base-install check.
- Use `scripts/benchmark_diagram.py` for reproducible worker timing without a web server; it retains the source snapshot, settings, result, logs, and `benchmark.json` under the run directory. `scripts/check_phase_workflow.py` exercises a supplied assessment against a running server. Compare like-for-like settings and source checksums, and report unresolved coverage alongside performance; a fast completed job is not a validated phase diagram.
- Test meaningful behavior: composition conversion, database suitability, phase mapping, scientific benchmark outputs, persistence, and error handling.
- Use small redistributable fixtures; avoid network calls in ordinary tests.
- Scientific regression tests need documented tolerances and references, not exact floating-point equality.
- The current UI lets users select databases; it does not automatically establish assessment suitability or verify validity ranges. Explain source limitations, and preserve manual selection if adding reliable recommendations.
- Build accessible forms and keyboard navigation; label physical units and distinguish warnings from calculation failures.
- Keep UI copy concise. Avoid stacks of subtitles, numbered eyebrow headings, repeated preview disclaimers, and explanatory captions that repeat the controls. Use one page-level status label and add supporting text only when it helps a user make a decision or understand units, assumptions, or errors.
- Preserve reduced-motion behavior, smooth panel transitions, and counted stage fills. The inspector labels disagreements while keeping nearest-sample values available for other checks. Crystal-view changes must preserve sharp settled rendering on high-DPI desktop/mobile displays: use the wide lattice cache during the dive and rebuild visible layers at the settled view's pixel density. See `docs/ui-ux.md` for interface behavior.
- Do not display mock calculations as real results.
- Report what was implemented, what was checked, and remaining limitations. Do not claim planned integrations are operational.
